Contents The Problem: Finding Rows Fast How Tables Live on Disk The Idea of an Index B+ Trees, Drawn Out Building a B+ Tree by Hand How Tall Is the Tree? The Math Hash Indexes Clustered, Secondary, and Covering Indexes Composite Indexes and the Leftmost-Prefix Rule Selectivity: When the Index Is Ignored Reading EXPLAIN: A Hands-On Lab The Cost of Indexes on Writes LSM Trees: The Write-Friendly Alternative Scenario: The Slow "My Orders" Page Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. The Problem: Finding Rows Fast An online shop has an orders table with one million rows. A customer opens "My orders", and the app runs: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4242; Only 8 rows match. Without help, the database has no idea where those 8 rows are. It must read every row and check it. This is called a full table scan (PostgreSQL calls it a Seq Scan , short for sequential scan). On our test table this took about 26 ms. That sounds fast, but: The time grows with the table. At 100 million rows it is 100 times slower. Every scan pushes useful data out of memory and uses CPU that other queries need. If 500 users open the page per second, the database does 500 full scans per second. After adding one index, the same query took 0.096 ms . That is about 270 times faster, and the gap grows as the table grows. This page explains exactly why. 2. How Tables Live on Disk A database does not read single rows from disk. It reads fixed-size blocks called pages . In PostgreSQL a page is 8 KB. In MySQL's InnoDB engine it is 16 KB. One page holds many rows. orders table file (the "heap") +-----------+-----------+-----------+----- -----+-----------+ | page 0 | page 1 | page 2 | ... | page 7739 | | rows 1-129| rows ... | | | | +-----------+-----------+-----------+----- -----+-----------+ 7,740 pages x 8 KB = about 60 MB Our real table: 1,000,000 rows took 7,740 pages (60 MB) , so about 129 rows fit in each page. The heap is the name for this main table file. Rows sit in it in no special order, roughly in the order they were inserted. The key cost model: the time of a query is mostly about how many pages it touches . Reading a page from memory is cheap. Reading it from disk is much more expensive, and random reads (jumping around) cost more than sequential reads (one page after another). Hold on to this idea. Everything else follows from it. A full scan of our table touches all 7,740 pages to find 8 rows. That is the waste we want to remove. 3. The Idea of an Index Intuition: the index at the back of a textbook. Words are listed in sorted order, and each word points to page numbers. To find "deadlock", you do not read the whole book. You jump to "D", find the word, and go straight to pages 212 and 340. A database index is a separate data structure that stores the values of one or more columns in sorted order. Each entry points to where the full row lives. In PostgreSQL that pointer is called a TID (tuple ID): a (page number, slot number) pair. index on customer_id (sorted) heap (unsorted) +-------------+------------+ | customer_id | points to | page 12: ... row for 4242 ... +-------------+------------+ page 803: ... row for 4242 ... | 4241 | (55, 3) | page 5120:... row for 4242 ... | 4242 | (12, 7) | ------ | 4242 | (803, 1) | ------ | 4242 | (5120, 9) | ------ | 4243 | (77, 2) | +-------------+------------+ Since the index is sorted, we can find a value with binary search : look at the middle, throw away the half that cannot contain the value, repeat. For one million sorted values, that takes at most log 2 (1,000,000) 20 steps instead of one million. But a plain sorted array has two problems on disk. Inserting a value in the middle means shifting everything after it. And each binary search step may land on a differ

pages.text: SQL Joins & How the Database Executes Them SQL joins from zero: inner, left, right and full joins worked on a tiny table, why a missing ON clause explodes row counts, nested loop, hash and merge joins with measured times (a 2,000 by 10,000 nested loop took 301... Contents Why Data Lives in More Than One Table Words You Need Four Join Shapes, Worked by Hand Cross Joins: When the Row Count Explodes Algorithm 1: Nested Loop Join Algorithm 2: Hash Join Algorithm 3: Merge Join The Lab: Measured Times Reading the Plan Join Order and Many Tables Exists, In, and Anti-Joins NULL Keys Do Not Match Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet 1. Why Data Lives in More Than One Table Suppose you store every order like this: order_id customer_name customer_city product amount 1 Ada Pune mug 400 2 Ada Pune book 250 3 Dev Delhi mug 400 Ada's city is stored twice. If she moves, you must update every row. Miss one, and the same person lives in two cities. That is the update anomaly that normalization is designed to stop. The usual fix is to split the data and point at it: customers orders id name city id customer_id product amount 1 Ada Pune 1 1 mug 400 2 Dev Delhi 2 1 book 250 3 2 mug 400 Ada's city now lives in one place. To print "who bought what, and from which city?" the database must join the two tables on orders.customer_id = customers.id . Intuition. A join is the reverse of a careful split. You split so each fact is stored once. You join so a question that needs two facts can still be answered in one result. 2. Words You Need Join key. The column (or columns) that say "these two rows belong together." Here, customer_id and id . Inner join. Keep a result row only when both sides have a match. Left (outer) join. Keep every row from the left table. If the right side has no match, fill those columns with NULL (a marker that means "unknown / not present"). Right join. The mirror of a left join. Most people write a left join and swap the table order instead. Full (outer) join. Keep rows from either side, with NULLs where the other side is missing. Cross join. Every row of A paired with every row of B. Row count is |A| |B| . Cardinality. How many rows a step produces. A join can shrink a result, or blow it up. Selectivity. How picky a condition is. "customer_id = 42" is selective. "amount 0" often is not. Nested loop, hash, and merge join. The three algorithms the engine uses to actually find matching pairs. The SQL you write does not name them. The planner picks one. You read the choice in EXPLAIN . Build side and probe side. In a hash join, the engine builds a hash table from one input (usually the smaller one) and probes it with the other. 3. Four Join Shapes, Worked by Hand Here is a tiny company. We will use it for the rest of this section. employees teams id name team_id id name 1 Ada 10 10 Design 2 Bilal 10 20 Ops 3 Chen 20 30 Research 4 Diya NULL Diya has no team. Research has no people. Inner join SELECT e.name, t.name AS team FROM employees e JOIN teams t ON e.team_id = t.id; Walk each employee, look up the team, keep the row only if a team exists: Ada + 10 - Design keep (Ada, Design) Bilal + 10 - Design keep (Bilal, Design) Chen + 20 - Ops keep (Chen, Ops) Diya + NULL - no match drop Result: three rows. Diya is gone. Research is gone. JOIN with no extra word means INNER JOIN . The two spellings are the same. Left join SELECT e.name, t.name AS team FROM employees e LEFT JOIN teams t ON e.team_id = t.id; Ada + Design Bilal + Design Chen + Ops Diya + NULL - kept, with no team name Four rows. Every employee is there. This is the usual way to ask "list people, and their team if they have one." Right join SELECT e.name, t.name AS team FROM employees e RIGHT JOIN teams t ON e.team_id = t.id; Ada + Design Bilal + Design Chen + Ops NULL + Research - the team with no people Diya is gone, because she is on the left and this join is driven by the right table. The same result is usually written as a left join with the tables swapped: SELECT e

The Big Picture: One Big Table A small shop starts by keeping orders in one spreadsheet. Every row is "one product in one order": order_id order_date customer_id customer_name customer_city product_id product_name unit_price qty 101 2026-11-01 7 Asha Pune P1 Pen 20 3 101 2026-11-01 7 Asha Pune P2 Notebook 60 2 102 2026-11-02 9 Ravi Mysuru P1 Pen 20 1 102 2026-11-02 9 Ravi Mysuru P3 Bag 900 1 103 2026-11-05 7 Asha Pune P2 Notebook 60 5 It is easy to read. It is also full of repetition : "Asha, Pune" appears 3 times, and "Notebook, 60" appears twice. With 10,000 orders, Asha's city might be stored hundreds of times. Repetition by itself only wastes space. The real problem is that every copy is a chance for the copies to disagree . Once two rows say different things about the same fact, the database no longer knows the truth. Normalization is a step-by-step method for splitting a table so that each fact is stored in exactly one place . The steps are called normal forms : 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, and so on. Each one removes one kind of repetition. Intuition: a well-designed table is about one thing. A customers table is about customers. A products table is about products. The big table above is about four things at once, which is why it breaks. 2. Three Ways the Big Table Breaks An anomaly is a case where a normal change to the data causes a wrong or impossible result. The big table has all three kinds. Update anomaly Asha moves to Bengaluru. You must change three rows. If the app updates only the rows for her latest order, the table now says she lives in two cities at once. Which one is true? Nobody knows. Insert anomaly The shop adds a new product, P4 "Stapler", price 150. Nobody has ordered it yet. To add a row you need an order_id , but there is no order. You cannot store the product without inventing a fake order. Delete anomaly Ravi cancels order 102, so you delete its two rows. Order 102 was the only order with the Bag. Now the fact "P3 is a Bag that costs 900" is gone too. Deleting one fact destroyed a different fact. All three come from the same cause: facts about customers and products are stored inside rows about order lines . Normalization fixes the cause, and the anomalies disappear with it. 3. Keys, in Plain Words A relation is the textbook word for a table. An attribute is a column. A tuple is a row. This page mostly uses the everyday words. Term Plain meaning In the big table Superkey Any set of columns whose values are never the same in two rows. It picks out exactly one row. {order_id, product_id}, and also {order_id, product_id, qty} Candidate key A superkey with nothing extra: remove any column and it stops being unique. {order_id, product_id} Primary key The one candidate key you choose to identify rows. (order_id, product_id) Composite key A key made of more than one column. (order_id, product_id) is composite Prime attribute A column that is part of some candidate key. order_id, product_id Foreign key A column that points to the primary key of another table. The database checks the target exists. (appears after we split: orders.customer_id customers) Surrogate key A made-up ID with no meaning, such as an auto-increment number or a UUID. customer_id = 7 Natural key A key that has real-world meaning,

pages.text: Replication, Sharding & the CAP Theorem Distributed databases from zero: why one database server is not enough, leader and follower replication, synchronous vs asynchronous copies, replication lag and stale reads, failover and split brain, quorums (W + R >... Contents Why One Server Is Not Enough The Words, in Plain English Leader and Followers: How Copies Are Made Synchronous vs Asynchronous: When Is a Write "Done"? Replication Lag and Stale Reads Failover and Split Brain Leaderless Replication and Quorums Sharding: Splitting the Data Consistent Hashing (Real Experiment) Hot Keys and Cross-Shard Queries The CAP Theorem and PACELC Worked Design: Growing a Shop's Database Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet 1. Why One Server Is Not Enough Picture a small online shop. It has one PostgreSQL server. Everything works. Then the shop grows, and three different problems show up: It breaks. The disk fails, or the cloud restarts the machine. While it is down, nobody can buy anything. One machine is a single point of failure : one broken part stops everything. Too many reads. Thousands of people browse products. Most queries only read . The one server's CPU is at 100%. Too much data or too many writes. The orders table no longer fits on one disk, or one machine cannot write fast enough. Each problem has a different fix: Problem Fix Idea Server breaks Replication Keep a full copy on another machine, ready to take over Too many reads Replication Send reads to the copies Too much data, too many writes Sharding Split the data across machines; each holds a part Intuition. Replication is photocopying a book so several people can read it, and so you still have it if one copy is lost. Sharding is splitting an encyclopedia into volumes A-F, G-M, and so on, because no single shelf can hold it all. Big systems do both: they split the data into shards, and keep copies of each shard. Before you reach for either, remember the cheaper steps: add an index , fix slow queries, add a cache, or buy a bigger machine (called scaling up or vertical scaling ). Adding more machines is called scaling out or horizontal scaling . Scaling out is powerful, but it makes everything harder, as this page will show. 2. The Words, in Plain English Word Meaning Node One machine (or one database process) in the group. Replica A copy of the data on one node. Leader (also primary, master) The one node that accepts writes. Follower (also replica, standby, secondary) A node that copies changes from the leader. It can serve reads. Replication lag How far behind the leader a follower is, in time or in bytes of log. Failover Making a follower the new leader when the old leader dies. Network partition The network breaks so that some nodes cannot talk to others, while each side is still running. Shard (also partition) One slice of the data. Each row lives in exactly one shard. Shard key The column used to decide which shard a row goes to, for example customer_id . Consistency (in CAP) Every read sees the latest write, as if there were only one copy. Availability (in CAP) Every request to a working node gets an answer (not an error). Note: "consistency" in CAP is not the C in ACID. ACID's C means "the data follows its rules" (for example, a balance is never negative). CAP's C means "all copies look like one copy". Same word, two meanings. 3. Leader and Followers: How Copies Are Made The most common setup is single-leader replication . One node is the leader. All writes go to it. The leader sends every change to the followers, and they apply the changes in the same order. writes reads app ───────────────────► LEADER ◄──────────── app │ change log (WAL) │ sent in order ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ FOLLOWER 1 FOLLOWER 2 FOLLOWER 3 ▲ ▲ ▲ └──── reads ────┴──── reads ─────┘ What exactly is sent? The Idea: Many Rows In, Fewer Rows Out A table of orders may have millions of rows. A manager does not want to read them. They want a few numbers. SQL has two tools for that: GROUP BY (aggregation) window function many rows - one row per group many rows - the SAME rows, each with an extra Pune 300 \ column computed Pune 200 \ from its group Pune 700 Pune 2300 Pune 400 / Pune 300 | Pune total 2300 Pune 700 / Pune 200 | Pune total 2300 Pune 700 | Pune total 2300 Delhi 500 \ ... Delhi 100 Delhi 600 Delhi NULL/ GROUP BY squashes each group into one row. A window function keeps every row and adds a value computed over related rows. Most real reports need one or the other, and many need both. 2. Words You Need Aggregate function. A function that takes many values and returns one: COUNT , SUM , AVG , MIN , MAX . Group. A set of rows that share the same value in the GROUP BY columns. NULL. SQL's "unknown" or "missing" value. It is not zero and not an empty string. Window. The set of rows a window function looks at for the current row. Partition. A window function's version of a group: PARTITION BY city means "look only at rows with the same city". Unlike GROUP BY , rows are not squashed. Frame. A sliding part of the partition, like "from the first row up to this one" (for running totals) or "the 2 rows before this one and this one" (for moving averages). Correlated subquery. A query inside a query that uses a value from the outer row, so it runs again for every outer row. 3. The Sample Table Every result on this page was produced by running the query in SQLite 3.46. Contents Why Transactions Exist ACID in Plain Words Atomicity and Durability: the Write-Ahead Log Concurrency Anomalies, One Timeline Each Isolation Levels MVCC: How Readers and Writers Stop Blocking Each Other Locks, Two-Phase Locking, and Deadlocks Hands-On Lab: Reproduce It in PostgreSQL Scenario: The Double-Booked Seat Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. Why Transactions Exist Moving 100 from Alice to Bob takes two writes: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE owner = 'alice'; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE owner = 'bob'; Two things can go wrong: Failure in the middle. The server crashes after the first line. Alice lost 100, Bob got nothing. Money vanished. Interference. While this runs, another request reads both balances and sees the "in between" state, or changes Alice's balance at the same moment. A transaction groups several operations into one logical unit. Either all of them happen or none do, and concurrent transactions are kept from stepping on each other. BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE owner = 'alice'; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE owner = 'bob'; COMMIT; -- make it permanent -- or ROLLBACK; to undo everything since BEGIN 2. ACID in Plain Words Letter Promise How databases keep it A tomicity All or nothing. A half-done transaction never stays. Undo information and the write-ahead log; on crash, unfinished work is discarded C onsistency A transaction takes the data from one valid state to another valid state. Constraints ( NOT NULL , UNIQUE , CHECK , foreign keys) plus your application logic I solation Concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work, as if they ran one at a time (to a configurable degree). Locks and/or MVCC snapshots D urability Once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash or power loss. Flushing the log to stable storage ( fsync ) before acknowledging commit; replication Note: the "C" is partly your job. The database cannot know that "total money must stay constant" unless you encode it. A CHECK (balance = 0) constraint is something it can enforce for you. 3. Atomicity and Durability: the Write-Ahead Log Data files are big and written in pages (8 KiB in PostgreSQL, 16 KiB in InnoDB). Writing every changed page to disk at every commit would be slow and random. Instead, databases use a write-ahead log (WAL) , also called a redo log or journal. The one rule Before a changed data page is written to disk, the log record describing that change must already be on disk. Commit, step by step The transaction changes pages in memory (the buffer pool). They are now "dirty". Each change also appends a small record to the WAL buffer: "in page 42, slot 3, balance 500 became 400". On COMMIT , the database appends a commit record and flushes the WAL up to that point with fsync . The log is sequential, so this is fast. Only now does COMMIT return success to the client. Dirty data pages are written later, in the background, at a checkpoint . Crash recovery After a crash, the database reads the WAL from the last checkpoint and redoes every logged change. Transactions with a commit record are restored (durability). Transactions without one never become visible (atomicity): in PostgreSQL their row versions are simply ignored as "aborted"; in InnoDB they are rolled back using the undo log. Intuition: the WAL is a chef's order slip. Before cooking anything, the order is written down. If the kitchen catches fire, you rebuild from the slips. Writing a slip is much faster than finishing the dish, so you can promise the customer "your order is safe" early. Contents Why Concurrency Is Hard A Race Condition, Step by Step Critical Sections and the Three Rules Atomic Instructions: Help From the Hardware Mutexes and Spinlocks Semaphores Condition Variables and Monitors Three Classic Problems Deadlock: The Four Conditions Handling Deadlock: Prevent, Avoid, Detect The Banker's Algorithm, Worked by Hand Starvation, Livelock, and Priority Inversion Scenario: The Frozen Payments Service Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. Why Concurrency Is Hard Concurrency means several tasks are in progress at the same time. They may truly run at the same moment on different CPU cores (this is called parallelism ), or one core may switch between them very fast. Either way, you do not control the exact order in which their steps happen. That is fine when tasks share nothing. Trouble starts when two threads (two paths of execution inside one program) read and write the same memory. The result can depend on timing. A bug that depends on timing may show up once in a million runs, vanish when you add a print statement, and then appear in production on a busy day. Intuition: Two people share one notebook that holds a bank balance. Each one reads the number, does the math in their head, and writes the new number. If they both read "100" before either writes, and each adds 50, both write "150". One deposit is lost. Nobody did anything wrong alone. The bug lives in the overlap . This page gives you the words and tools to reason about that overlap: Race condition: the result depends on the timing of threads. Synchronization: rules and tools that control the order threads may run in. Deadlock: threads wait for each other forever because of those very rules. 2. A Race Condition, Step by Step Here is a tiny C program. Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter one million times. The right answer is 2,000,000. #include pthread.h #include stdio.h long counter = 0; void *work(void *arg) { for (int i = 0; i 1000000; i++) { counter++; /* load, add, store: NOT atomic */ } return NULL; } int main(void) { pthread_t a, b; pthread_create( and a, NULL, work, NULL); pthread_create( and b, NULL, work, NULL); pthread_join(a, NULL); pthread_join(b, NULL); printf("counter = %ld (expected 2000000)\n", counter); return 0; } Compile with gcc -O0 -pthread race.c -o race and run it three times. On an 8-core Linux machine we got: counter = 1156636 (expected 2000000) counter = 1109601 (expected 2000000) counter = 1026926 (expected 2000000) Almost half the updates vanished, and the number changes every run. Why? counter++ is really three steps The CPU cannot change memory in place for this line. It does three separate steps: Load: copy counter from memory into a register (a tiny storage slot inside the CPU). Add: add 1 to the register. Store: write the register back to memory. A thread can be paused, or another core can act, between any two steps. Here is one bad interleaving (an order in which the steps of two threads mix together). The counter starts at 5. Time Thread A Thread B counter in memory 1 load 5 into register 5 2 load 5 into register 5 3 add: register = 6 5 4 add: register = 6 5 5 store 6 6 6 store 6 6 (should be 7) Both threads did one increment, but the counter only went up by one. This is called a lost update . The same bug exists in databases , where two transactions read and then write the same row. How to spot a race: look for shared data + at least one writer + no rule that orders the accesses . All three must be true. Remove any one of them and the race is gone. Try it yourself: count the outcomes Two threads each run x = x + 1 once, starting from x = 0 . Each is load, add, store. What final values are possible? Contents Why Caches Exist: the Speed Gap The Memory Hierarchy and Locality Cache Lines: Memory Moves in 64-Byte Blocks Measuring the Hierarchy Yourself Where Can a Line Go? Direct-Mapped and Set-Associative Splitting an Address by Hand The Three Kinds of Misses and AMAT What Happens on a Write Loop Order: a 10x Speedup from Two Lines Many Cores: Coherence and MESI False Sharing: Slow Without Sharing Anything NUMA: Near and Far Memory How This Connects to the Rest Practice Problems Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. Why Caches Exist: the Speed Gap A modern CPU core can do a simple step (add two numbers) in well under a nanosecond. But fetching one number from main memory ( RAM ) takes around 80 to 150 nanoseconds. In that time the core could have done hundreds of steps. If every read went to RAM, the CPU would spend almost all its time waiting. The fix is a cache : a small, very fast memory that sits on the CPU chip and keeps copies of data that was used recently. When the data you need is in the cache, that is a hit , and it is fast. When it is not, that is a miss : the CPU must fetch it from a slower level, and it waits. Intuition: Think of studying for an exam. The book you are reading is on your desk (cache). Other books are on the shelf across the room (RAM). Books you have not opened this year are in the library across town (disk). You keep the books you use most on the desk, because walking to the shelf every time would waste the whole evening. Fast memory is expensive and takes chip space, so we cannot make the cache as big as RAM. Instead, computers stack several levels, each one bigger and slower than the one before. That stack is the memory hierarchy . 2. The Memory Hierarchy and Locality faster, smaller, costlier per byte ^ +-----------------+ | ~0.3 ns a few hundred bytes (inside the core) | Registers | | +-----------------+ | | L1 cache | | ~1 ns 32-64 KiB per core +-----------------+ | | L2 cache | | ~4 ns 1-2 MiB per core +-----------------+ | | L3 cache | | ~10-40 ns tens to hundreds of MiB, shared by all cores +-----------------+ | | RAM (DRAM) | | ~80-150 ns gigabytes +-----------------+ | | SSD / disk | | ~20-100 us (SSD), ~5-10 ms (spinning disk) +-----------------+ v slower, bigger, cheaper per byte These are rough, typical numbers. Your machine will differ a bit, and section 4 shows how to measure your own. Caches work because real programs are not random. They show locality : Temporal locality (locality in time): if you used a piece of data just now, you will probably use it again soon. Example: a loop counter, or the top of the stack. Spatial locality (locality in space): if you used one address, you will probably use the addresses right next to it soon. Example: walking through an array from start to end. Caches use temporal locality by keeping recent data, and spatial locality by fetching data in blocks , not single bytes. That block is the next idea. 3. Cache Lines: Memory Moves in 64-Byte Blocks The cache never fetches just one byte. It fetches a whole cache line (also called a cache block). On almost all current x86 and ARM CPUs a line is 64 bytes . When you read one byte, the 63 bytes around it come along for free. RAM addresses (each box = 4 bytes = one int) line 0: [a0][a1][a2][a3][a4][a5][a6][a7][a8][a9][a10][a11][a12][a13][a14][a15] bytes 0-63 line 1: [a16][a17] ... [a31] bytes 64-127 Read a0 - MISS, the whole line 0 (a0..a15) is copied into the cache Read a1 - HIT (already there) ... Read a15 - HIT Read a16 - MISS, line 1 is fetched Worked example: counting misses in a sum You sum an array of 1,000,000 int values (4 bytes each, so 4,000,000 bytes) from start to end. The cache starts empty. How many misses? Ints per line = 64 / 4 = 16 . Lines tou

The Big Picture: the I/O Stack A disk only understands one thing: "read or write block number N". It has no idea what a file, a folder, or a name is. A file system is the part of the operating system that builds files and folders on top of those numbered blocks. Common ones are ext4 and XFS on Linux, APFS on macOS, and NTFS on Windows. I/O means input/output: moving data in or out of the program, for example to a disk or a network. When your program calls write() , the data passes down through several layers: your program write(fd, "hello", 5) | (a system call: a request to the kernel) -----+---------------------------------------------------------- user space / kernel v VFS one common front door for every file system | page cache copies of file data kept in RAM (section 7) | file system (ext4) maps "byte 5,000,000 of notes.txt" to "block 81,233" | and keeps the journal (sections 6, 9) block layer queues and merges requests, picks an order | device driver speaks NVMe, SATA, or a cloud disk protocol v disk (SSD/HDD) stores bits. Has its own small cache too. A system call (syscall) is how a program asks the kernel to do something it is not allowed to do itself, such as touching hardware. See Processes and Threads for user space and kernel space. The VFS (Virtual File System) is a shared layer that gives every file system the same set of operations: open, read, write, close. That is why the same cat works on ext4, on a USB stick, and on a network share. The most important idea on this page: most layers lie a little to be fast . The page cache says "done" before the data reaches the disk. The disk may say "done" while the data is still in its own cache. Section 8 shows how to get the truth when you need it. 2. Disks: Blocks, HDDs, and SSDs Storage is cut into fixed-size pieces: A sector is the smallest piece the hardware reads or writes. Usually 512 bytes or 4 KiB. A block is the smallest piece the file system hands out. On ext4 it is almost always 4 KiB (4,096 bytes). Even a 6-byte file uses one whole 4 KiB block. A KiB is 1,024 bytes. (KB is sometimes 1,000 bytes. With disks the difference adds up, so this page uses KiB, MiB, GiB.) Hard disks and solid-state drives HDD (spinning disk) SSD (NVMe flash) RAM, for comparison How it works A metal plate spins. An arm moves a head to the right track and waits for the data to spin under it. Flash memory chips. No moving parts. Electronic memory, lost on power off One random 4 KiB read about 5 10 ms about 0.05 0.1 ms (50 100 s) about 0.0001 ms (100 ns) Random reads per second (IOPS) about 100 200 hundreds of thousands Reading in order (sequential) about 150 250 MiB/s about 2 7 GiB/s tens of GiB/s IOPS means I/O operations per second: how many separate small reads or writes a disk can do each second. Throughput is how many bytes per second it can move. Worked example: random versus sequential You must read 10,000 small 4 KiB records (40 MiB in total) from an HDD. Scattered randomly: 10,000 reads 8 ms = 80 seconds . Stored next to each other: 40 MiB 200 MiB/s = 0.2 seconds . That is 400 times faster. On an SSD the random case is about 10,000 0.08 ms = 0.8 s, so the gap is much smaller, but sequential access still wins. This is why databases log changes by appending to

pages.text: I/O Models & Event Loops How one program serves thousands of network clients: blocking vs non-blocking I/O, threads vs event loops, select, poll and epoll, level vs edge triggering, a hand-written event loop, async/await, measured results (200... Contents The Problem: Programs Mostly Wait Words You Need Model 1: One Thread, Blocking Model 2: One Thread per Client Non-Blocking Sockets: "Not Ready Yet" Asking the Kernel: select, poll, epoll An Event Loop by Hand Level-Triggered vs Edge-Triggered async/await: Event Loops Made Readable The Lab: Four Servers, 200 Clients The Classic Bug: Blocking the Loop Real Servers Mix Models Backpressure: When Clients Are Slow Practice Problems Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. The Problem: Programs Mostly Wait Look at one request to a typical API: receive request ~0.05 ms of CPU parse JSON ~0.05 ms of CPU ask the database ~5 ms of WAITING (network + database work) build the reply ~0.1 ms of CPU send the reply ~0.05 ms of CPU (more waiting if the client is slow) The CPU is busy for about 0.25 ms. The request takes about 5.25 ms. So the CPU is idle about 95% of the time for this request. If the program does nothing else while it waits, 95% of the machine is wasted. Intuition. Think of a waiter in a restaurant. A bad waiter takes one order, walks to the kitchen, and stands there until the food is ready. A good waiter takes the order to the kitchen and goes to the next table. The kitchen rings a bell when food is ready. The good waiter is an event loop , and the bell is epoll . There are two big ways to use the waiting time: Many workers. Use many threads. When one thread waits, the operating system runs another one. One clever worker. Use one thread that never waits on a single client. It keeps a list of all clients and only works on the ones that are ready. 2. Words You Need Word Plain meaning I/O Input/output: reading or writing data that lives outside the CPU and memory, such as a network socket, a disk file, or a keyboard. Socket The program's end of a network connection. You read bytes from it and write bytes to it (see TCP: sockets ). File descriptor (fd) A small number the kernel gives your program for each open file or socket, like a ticket number: 0, 1, 2, 3... System call A request from your program to the kernel, such as read , write , accept . Each one costs a little time (roughly 0.1 to 1 microsecond). Blocking call A call that puts your thread to sleep until it can finish. recv() on an empty socket blocks until data arrives. Non-blocking call A call that returns at once. If it cannot finish, it says "try again later" (the error EAGAIN ). Ready A socket is "ready to read" when a read would not block (data is waiting). It is "ready to write" when there is room in the kernel's send buffer. Event loop A loop that asks the kernel "which sockets are ready?", handles each ready one a little, and asks again. Forever. Concurrency Many tasks are in progress at the same time (they take turns). Parallelism means tasks really run at the same instant on different CPU cores. An event loop gives concurrency on one core. 3. Model 1: One Thread, Blocking The simplest server. One thread does everything, one client at a time: while True: conn = sock.accept() # sleep until a client connects data = conn.recv(64) # sleep until the client sends something reply = handle(data) # maybe sleep again on the database conn.sendall(reply) # sleep if the client reads slowly conn.close() Each line can block. While the thread waits for client A's database answer, client B is stuck in the kernel's queue of not-yet-accepted connections (the listen backlog ). Worked example 200 clients arrive at the same moment. Each request waits 100 ms on the database. The server handles them one after another: Client 1 finishes at 100 ms. Client 2 at 200 ms. Client k at k 100 ms. The last client finishes at 200 100 ms = 20 s . The middle client (the median, p50) waits about 100 100 ms = 10 s . The CPU did almost nothing during those 20 s

Contents Why This Matters Words You Need The Memory Map of a Process The Stack, Traced by Hand The Heap: How malloc and free Work Fragmentation Lab: Speed and Fragmentation in C Bugs of Manual Memory Reference Counting Tracing GC: Mark and Sweep by Hand Generational GC Lab: Python's Collector at Work Java, Go, Node and Rust GC in Production and in Containers Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution 1. Why This Matters Three real problems come straight from this topic: A service frees most of its data after a busy hour, but its memory graph never goes down. The team thinks it is a leak. It is not. It is fragmentation (section 6). A Java or Go API has a fine average latency, but every few seconds a request takes 300 ms. That is often a garbage collection pause (section 11). A container is killed with OOMKilled even though the language runtime "thinks" it has plenty of room. The runtime did not know about the container limit (section 14, and the OOMKilled scenario ). You can only fix these if you know where memory comes from and who gives it back. 2. Words You Need Allocate. Ask for a piece of memory to hold some data. Free (or release ). Say "I am done with this piece; it can be reused." Stack. A region of memory for function calls. Each call gets a slice; the slice is thrown away when the call returns. Fast and automatic, but small. Heap. A big region for data that must live longer than one function call, or whose size is only known at run time. You (or a garbage collector) must free it. Allocator. The code that hands out heap memory. In C it is malloc and free , usually from glibc on Linux. Pointer (or reference ). A value that holds the address of some data. "A points to B" means A knows where B lives. Leak. Memory you no longer need but never freed. It stays used until the process dies. Garbage. Heap data that nothing can reach any more. No pointer leads to it. Garbage collector (GC). Code inside a language runtime that finds garbage and frees it for you. RSS (resident set size). How much real RAM a process is using right now. This is what top shows and what container limits count. Pause (or stop-the-world ). A moment when the GC stops your code so it can work safely. 3. The Memory Map of a Process From virtual memory you know that each process sees its own private address space. Here is how that space is laid out on Linux, low addresses at the bottom: high addresses +-----------------------------+ | stack | grows DOWN, one frame per call | | | (default limit often 8 MB per thread) | v | | | | mmap area | big malloc blocks, shared libraries, | | memory-mapped files | ^ | | | | | heap | grows UP (brk), small malloc blocks +-----------------------------+ | data / bss | global variables +-----------------------------+ | text | your machine code (read-only) +-----------------------------+ low addresses You can see this for any running process: cat /proc/ pid /maps lists every region, and [heap] and [stack] are labeled. The stack limit is shown by ulimit -s (in KB). 4. The Stack, Traced by Hand Each function call gets a stack frame : a slice of the stack that holds its local variables, its arguments, and the address to go back to when it returns. Take this C code: int square(int x) { int r = x * x; return r; } int main(void) { int a = 3; int b = square(a); return b; } Here is the stack at each step. Each box is a frame; the newest frame is on top. step 1: main starts step 2: main calls square step 3: square returns +--------------------+ | square | | x = 3 | | r = 9 | | return to main | +------------------+ +--------------------+ +------------------+ | main | | main | | main | | a = 3 | | a = 3 | | a = 3 | | b = ? | |

pages.text: Processes, Threads & CPU Scheduling Operating systems from zero: what a process is, process states, context switches, fork and exec, threads, CPU scheduling algorithms with fully worked examples, Linux EEVDF and sched_ext, and container CPU throttling. Contents The Big Picture What Is a Process? Process States Context Switches Creating Processes: fork, exec, wait Threads Scheduling Vocabulary Scheduling Algorithms, Worked by Hand How Linux Actually Schedules (CFS, EEVDF, sched_ext) Scenario: Why Is My Container Slow at 30% CPU? Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet Try it live: Run FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin and Priority on your own processes and compare waiting times. Open the CPU Scheduling Simulator lab 1. The Big Picture Your laptop may have 8 CPU cores. Yet it runs a browser, a music player, a chat app, and hundreds of background services at once. How? The answer is time sharing . The operating system (OS) gives each program a tiny slice of CPU time, a few milliseconds. Then it pauses that program and gives the CPU to another one. It switches so fast that, to a human, everything looks simultaneous. To do this, the OS needs answers to three questions: What exactly is a "running program"? That is a process (and inside it, threads ). How do we pause one program and resume another without losing anything? That is a context switch . Who runs next, and for how long? That is CPU scheduling . Intuition: Think of one chef (the CPU) and many recipes being cooked (processes). The chef works on one dish for a minute, writes a sticky note saying exactly where they stopped ("added salt, stirring step 4"), then moves to another dish. The sticky note is the saved context. The rule for choosing the next dish is the scheduler. 2. What Is a Process? A program is a file on disk, for example /usr/bin/python3 . It is passive. It does nothing by itself. A process is a program in execution . It is the program plus everything needed to run it right now. If you open three terminal windows and run python3 in each, you have one program and three processes. What a process owns A process ID (PID): a number that names it, for example 4182. Its own virtual address space: its private view of memory. Process A cannot read process B's memory by accident. CPU state: the values in the CPU registers, including the program counter (the address of the next instruction to run) and the stack pointer . Open resources: open files, network sockets, pipes. Each is referenced by a small number called a file descriptor (0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr). Credentials and limits: which user it runs as, how much memory it may use, and so on. The kernel stores all of this in a data structure called the Process Control Block (PCB) . In Linux the PCB is struct task_struct . The memory layout of a process High addresses +--------------------------+ | Stack | local variables, function call frames | grows downward v | (one stack per thread) | | | (free space) | | | | grows upward ^ | | Heap | malloc / new / Python objects +--------------------------+ | BSS | global variables that start as zero | Data | global variables with initial values +--------------------------+ | Text (code) | the machine instructions, read-only +--------------------------+ Low addresses Every address in this picture is virtual . The OS and hardware translate it to real RAM. See Virtual Memory and Paging for how. You can look at a live process on Linux: $ cat /proc/self/status | head -n 9 # info about the 'cat' process itself $ ls -l /proc/$$/fd # open file descriptors of your shell $ cat /proc/$$/maps # its memory regions (text, heap, stack, libraries) 3. Process States A process is not always running. At any moment it is in one of a few states: admitted exit() [ NEW ] ----------- [ READY ] ----+ [ TERMINATED ] | ^ | ^ scheduler picks | | time | | it v | slice | | [ RUNNING ] ----+-----------+ | used up / preempted waits for I/O, | a lock, or sleep v [ WAITING ] (also called BLOCKED) | +---- I/O done ----- back

pages.text: System Calls & the Kernel Boundary System calls from zero: user space vs kernel space, what happens in a trap, the main syscall families, and a lab that measured 2 million getpid calls at 66 ns each versus 0.28 ns for a userspace add, clock_gettime at 25... Contents Two Worlds: User Space and Kernel Space Words You Need What Happens During a System Call The Main Families The Lab: Measuring the Cost The vDSO: Some Calls Never Enter the Kernel Watching a Program Talk to the Kernel Too Many Syscalls: The N+1 I/O Problem How Errors Come Back Containers Can Limit Which Calls You Make Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet 1. Two Worlds: User Space and Kernel Space A CPU has a privilege switch. In everyday language: some instructions are allowed only for the operating system. The usual names are user mode (also called ring 3 on x86) and kernel mode (ring 0). user space kernel space +---------------------------+ +------------------------------+ | your process | | the operating system | | - your code and data | | - talks to devices | | - libraries (libc) | | - owns files, memory, net | | - cannot talk to disks | | - switches between processes| | or change page tables | | - enforces permissions | +--------------+------------+ +--------------^---------------+ | | | system call (a controlled door) | +----------------------------------+ This split is not a fashion. If every program could write any sector on the disk, or change any other process's memory, a bug in a calculator could wipe the machine. The kernel sits in the middle and allows only well-defined requests: "read this file," "send these bytes," "give me more memory." Intuition. Think of a bank. You cannot walk into the vault. You fill in a form at the counter (the system call). The teller (the kernel) checks your identity, does the work, and hands back a result or an error. The form is standardized. You cannot invent a new form that says "give me everyone else's money." 2. Words You Need System call (syscall). A request from a program to the kernel. On Linux, examples are read , write , open , mmap , fork , clone , poll , and getpid . User space. The memory and mode your process runs in. It cannot run privileged instructions. Kernel space. The memory and mode the operating system runs in. Trap (or exception, or software interrupt). The CPU event that switches from user mode to kernel mode in a controlled way. Modern x86-64 Linux uses the syscall instruction for this. ABI (application binary interface). The contract for how arguments are passed (which registers, which numbers identify which call) and how results come back. libc. The C library (on Linux often glibc or musl). Your Python or Go or Java program usually does not issue the raw instruction itself. A library wraps the syscall and gives you a function like open() or os.read() . vDSO (virtual dynamic shared object). A small page of kernel-provided code mapped into every process. A few "syscalls" run there, in user space, with no mode switch. clock_gettime is the usual example. Context switch. The kernel stops one thread and starts another. A syscall is not always a context switch to another process. Many syscalls run in the kernel and return to the same thread. A blocking syscall (wait for disk, wait for the network) often does cause a context switch, because the thread has nothing to do until the event arrives. File descriptor (fd). A small integer the kernel gives your process to refer to an open file, socket, or other object. See File Systems and Disk I/O . 3. What Happens During a System Call Suppose your program calls write(fd, buf, 13) to send hello, world\n . Under the hood, roughly this happens: 1. libc puts the syscall number for write in a register (on x86-64 Linux, rax = 1) and the arguments in others (rdi = fd, rsi = pointer to the bytes, rdx = 13). 2. It runs the syscall instruction. 3. The CPU switches to kernel mode, and jumps to a kernel entry point. User registers are saved. 4. The kernel checks the

pages.text: Virtual Memory & Paging Virtual memory from zero: address translation worked in hex, page tables, multi-level paging, TLBs, page faults, page replacement (FIFO, LRU, OPT) traced step by step, thrashing, huge pages, OOM kills, and how LLM... Contents Why Virtual Memory Exists Pages, Frames, and Offsets Translating an Address by Hand Page Table Size and Multi-Level Tables The TLB: Making Translation Fast Page Faults and Demand Paging Page Replacement: FIFO, LRU, OPT Thrashing and the Working Set Linux in Practice: Huge Pages, Overcommit, OOM Modern Twist: Paging for the LLM KV Cache Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. Why Virtual Memory Exists Imagine the early days: every program used real RAM addresses directly. Three problems appear immediately: No protection. A bug in one program can overwrite another program's data, or the OS itself. No relocation. A program compiled to live at address 0x10000 cannot run if another program already sits there. Fragmentation. Free RAM ends up in small scattered holes. A program needing 100 MB in one piece may fail even if 500 MB is free in total. Virtual memory solves all three with one idea: programs never see real addresses. Each process uses virtual addresses . The hardware (the MMU , Memory Management Unit, inside the CPU) translates each virtual address to a physical address in RAM on every memory access, using tables the OS maintains. Intuition: Virtual addresses are like apartment numbers in a building directory. "Apartment 4B" is what you tell your friends. The directory (page table) says 4B is actually the third door on the second floor of the east wing. The landlord (OS) can move you to another physical room and just update the directory. Your friends never notice. Bonus wins: processes can share read-only pages (one copy of libc in RAM for hundreds of processes), memory can be loaded lazily from disk, and a process can use more virtual memory than physical RAM exists. 2. Pages, Frames, and Offsets Translating every single byte separately would need a gigantic table. So memory is split into fixed-size chunks: A page is a fixed-size block of virtual memory. The common size is 4 KiB (4096 bytes). A frame (page frame) is a block of physical RAM of the same size. The page table maps page numbers to frame numbers. One entry per page is a PTE (page table entry). Because pages and frames are the same size, the position inside the page never changes during translation. So a virtual address splits in two parts: virtual address = [ virtual page number (VPN) | offset ] physical address = [ physical frame number (PFN) | offset ] (same offset) offset bits = log2(page size) 4 KiB = 2^12 - 12 offset bits A PTE stores more than the frame number. It has flag bits: present (is the page in RAM?), writable , user/kernel , accessed (used recently), dirty (modified since loaded), and on x86-64 an NX (no-execute) bit. 3. Translating an Address by Hand Setup: 32-bit virtual addresses, 4 KiB pages. So 12 bits of offset and 32 - 12 = 20 bits of VPN. Problem: translate virtual address 0x00403A7C . The page table says VPN 0x00403 maps to frame 0x001F2 , present. Step by step Split the address. 12 offset bits = 3 hex digits (each hex digit is 4 bits). So the last 3 hex digits are the offset: 0xA7C . The rest is the VPN: 0x00403 . Look up the VPN. PTE for 0x00403 gives PFN 0x001F2 . Present bit is 1, so no fault. Glue frame and offset. Physical address = PFN followed by the offset = 0x001F2 and A7C = 0x001F2A7C . In formula form: PA = PFN * page_size + offset = 0x1F2 * 0x1000 + 0xA7C = 0x1F2A7C . Shortcut: with 4 KiB pages the offset is exactly 3 hex digits, and with 64 KiB pages it is exactly 4, so you can split the address by counting hex digits from the right. For sizes like 8 KiB (13 offset bits), write the address in binary first. Try another (solution right below) Same system. pages.text: Scenario: Requests Stuck on Database Locks A real-world walkthrough of database lock trouble in PostgreSQL: requests that hang, a one-second migration that freezes every read, and deadlock errors. How lock queues work, finding the blocker with pg_stat_activity... Contents The Situation Words You Need How Lock Queues Work The Toolkit: Find the Blocker The Lab Incident 1: The Transaction That Never Ended Incident 2: The One-Second Migration That Froze Reads Incident 3: "deadlock detected" Retrying Safely The Same Problems in MySQL Prevention: Settings, Alerts, Reviews Blameless Postmortem Practice Problems Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. The Situation A shop's checkout API runs on 8 pods and talks to one PostgreSQL database. Over one week, on-call sees three strange problems: Monday 19:20 IST. Orders for one popular product hang for many seconds, then time out. Other products are fine. Wednesday 11:05 IST. A developer runs a migration that adds one column to the accounts table. It "should take a millisecond". For the next 8 seconds, every request that reads accounts hangs, including the login page. The error rate hits 40%. All week. The logs show a steady trickle of ERROR: deadlock detected from the wallet-transfer job, and some transfers fail. Dashboards show the database server is calm: low CPU, low disk use, plenty of memory. That is the first clue. When requests are slow but the database is idle , they are usually waiting , not working. The most common thing to wait for is a lock . 2. Words You Need Word Plain meaning Transaction A group of statements that succeed or fail together, between BEGIN and COMMIT (or ROLLBACK ). Lock A mark that says "I am using this; others must wait or share". Databases lock rows and tables. Row lock Taken by UPDATE , DELETE and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the rows they touch. Held until the transaction ends , not until the statement ends. Table lock A lock on a whole table. Every query takes a weak one (a plain SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE ). Schema changes like ALTER TABLE take the strongest one ( ACCESS EXCLUSIVE ), which conflicts with everything. Blocker The session holding the lock others want. Waiter A session that is stuck until the blocker lets go. Idle in transaction A session that started a transaction, ran some statements, and is now doing nothing, while still holding all its locks. Usually the app is busy elsewhere (an HTTP call) or forgot to commit. Deadlock Two or more transactions each wait for a lock the other holds. None can ever move. The database must kill one. Timeout A limit on how long to wait. PostgreSQL has several: lock_timeout , statement_timeout , idle_in_transaction_session_timeout . Intuition. A row lock is like taking a library book home. Nobody else can borrow it until you return it, even if you are not reading it right now. "Idle in transaction" is borrowing the book and then going on holiday. 3. How Lock Queues Work Two facts explain almost every lock incident. Fact 1: locks last until the transaction ends BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1; -- row 1 locked from here... -- app calls a payment API: 9 seconds COMMIT; -- ...to here The UPDATE took 0.1 ms. The lock lasted 9 seconds. Anyone else who wants to change row 1 waits those 9 seconds. Fact 2: waiters form a line, and the line is fair PostgreSQL serves lock requests roughly in arrival order. A new request will not jump ahead of an earlier waiter it conflicts with, even if the current holder would allow it. This stops strong locks from starving forever, but it has a nasty side effect: time ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────► long report: holds ACCESS SHARE on accounts (a slow SELECT inside a transaction) ALTER TABLE: wants ACCESS EXCLUSIVE ── waits for the report SELECT #1: wants ACCESS SHARE ── would fit with the report, but must wait BEHIND the ALTER SELECT #2: wants ACCESS SHARE ── also waits login page: ...everything that touches accounts waits The ALTER TABLE itself

Contents The Incident Words You Need The First Five Minutes Lab 1: Deleted, but Still Using Space Lab 2: Full With Space Left (Inodes) Other Reasons df and du Disagree Finding What Is Big The Usual Culprits The Database Case: WAL That Will Not Go Away Time-to-Full Math The Fix, in Order Prevention and Alerts Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution 1. The Incident 03:10 alert: api error rate 34% 03:11 api logs: OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device: '/var/lib/app/uploads/tmp...' 03:12 postgres: PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.123": No space left on device 03:14 on-call runs df -h: /dev/nvme0n1p1 100G 100G 0 100% / 03:16 on-call deletes /var/log/app/app.log (41 GB) 03:17 df -h still says 100%. Nothing changed. Two facts look impossible at 03:17. A 41 GB file was deleted and no space came back. Later, after things are fixed, du will say the whole disk only holds 52 GB of files, but df says 100 GB is used. Both make sense once you know how files are stored. Errno 28 ( ENOSPC ) is the error code behind "No space left on device", and you will see it from every program that tries to write. Why does a full disk break so much at once? Almost everything writes: databases write their log before every commit, apps write temp files and logs, package managers and containers unpack files. When the disk is full, all of them fail together, and often in confusing ways (a database may even shut itself down to protect your data). 2. Words You Need File system. The structure on a disk that stores files and folders (ext4, XFS, tmpfs). Each one is mounted at a folder, like / or /var/lib/docker . Block. The unit of disk space, usually 4 KB. A 1-byte file still uses one block. Inode. A small record for each file that holds its size, owner, permissions and where its blocks are. The file's name is not in the inode; names live in directories and point to inodes. Many file systems create a fixed number of inodes when they are formatted. Link count. How many names point to an inode. rm removes a name and lowers the count. The data is only freed when the count is 0 and no process has the file open. File descriptor. A number a process uses to refer to a file it has open. While a descriptor is open, the file's data stays, even with no name. df asks the file system "how many blocks are used in total?" du walks the folders, adds up the files it can find by name. They answer different questions. Ephemeral storage. In Kubernetes, the node's local disk that pods use for logs, writable container layers and emptyDir volumes. It disappears with the pod. 3. The First Five Minutes Do these in order. Each one takes seconds. # 1. which file system is full? (bytes) df -h # 2. is it really inodes? df -i # 3. which top-level folder is big? (-x: do not cross into other file systems) sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / 2 /dev/null | sort -h | tail -15 # 4. does du add up to much less than df? look for deleted-but-open files sudo lsof +L1 2 /dev/null | sort -k7 -n | tail # 5. what is still writing right now? sudo iotop -o -b -n 3 # or: pidstat -d 1 5 Step 1 tells you where . Step 2 tells you what kind of full. Step 3 finds normal big files. Step 4 finds the invisible ones. Step 5 tells you what will refill the disk two minutes after you clean it, which matters more than anything you delete. Priority. First, stop the bleeding: free a few GB safely so the database and app can write again (section 11). Then find the root cause. Do not start by deleting things you do not understand under /var/lib . 4. Lab 1: Deleted, but Still Using Space This is what happened at 03:16. Reading 502, 503 and 504, drawing the request path, the race between SIGTERM and load balancer updates, a runnable lab... Contents The Situation Read the Status Code: 502, 503, 504 Draw the Path a Request Takes Collect Clues: When, Where, How Many The Root Cause: Two Things Happen at Once Reproduce It: a Lab You Can Run The Results, Case by Case The Fix in Kubernetes Terms Graceful Shutdown in the App The Second Cause: Keep-Alive Timeout Races Should the Load Balancer Retry? Blameless Postmortem Preventing It: a Deploy Check in CI Practice Problems Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. The Situation The orders API runs on Kubernetes as a Deployment with 6 pods. Traffic comes in through a cloud load balancer, then an ingress controller (a proxy inside the cluster that routes HTTP requests to Services), then to the pods. On Thursday at 15:10 IST, a release goes out. The dashboard shows: 15:09 0 errors / min (normal) 15:10 release starts 15:10 41 x 502 / min 15:11 37 x 502 / min 15:12 0 errors / min (release finished) (These dashboard numbers are part of the story. The numbers measured by real code are in section 7 .) The same pattern shows up on every release, and also whenever the autoscaler removes pods at night. Customers sometimes see "Something went wrong" when they place an order. A few retried and were charged twice. 2. Read the Status Code: 502, 503, 504 Status codes in the 5xx range mean "the server side failed". But which server? When there is a proxy in front (and there almost always is), these three codes usually come from the proxy , describing what happened when it tried to talk to your app (the upstream ): Code Name What the proxy is saying Usual causes 502 Bad Gateway "I reached for the upstream, and the connection failed or the answer was broken." Connection refused (nothing listening), connection reset mid-request (the process died), upstream closed a keep-alive connection at the wrong moment 503 Service Unavailable "I have no healthy upstream to send this to," or the app itself says "I am overloaded." No ready pods in the Service, load shedding, maintenance 504 Gateway Timeout "I sent the request, and the upstream did not answer in time." Slow app, slow database, a firewall silently dropping packets (see the database scenario ) Intuition. A 502 means the connection to the app went wrong, not that the app's logic returned an error. If your app had a bug, you would see 500s written by the app. A burst of 502s that matches the deploy time points at pods starting or stopping . 3. Draw the Path a Request Takes user │ HTTPS ▼ cloud load balancer ──► ingress controller pods (nginx) │ picks a pod IP from the Service's │ endpoint list (keeps its own copy) ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ orders-1 orders-2 ... orders-6 (pod) (pod) (pod) The important detail: the ingress controller does not ask Kubernetes "which pods are ready?" on every request. It keeps its own copy of the list of pod IPs and updates it when Kubernetes tells it something changed. So does kube-proxy on every node, and so does the cloud load balancer if it sends traffic straight to pods. Each copy is updated a little later than the change. 4. Collect Clues: When, Where, How Many The on-call engineer checks four things, changing one question at a time: Which component wrote the 502? The ingress controller's access log has the line, with the upstream address and an upstream status of - (no answer). The app's own logs have nothing for those requests. So the proxy could not get an answer from a pod. Which pods? Every failing request went to a pod IP that was being shut down, or to one that had just been created. The error text. The ingress error log shows two kinds of message: connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream and upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from

pages.text: Scenario: A Pod Keeps Getting OOMKilled A real-world walkthrough: an API's Kubernetes pods restart every 40 minutes with OOMKilled and exit code 137. Telling OOMKilled apart from eviction, node OOM and grace-period kills; RSS, working set, anon and page... Contents The Situation Step 1: Read the Evidence Which Kind of Kill Is It? What "Memory" Means: RSS, Working Set, Anon, Cache Requests, Limits, QoS, and Who Dies First Step 2: Read the Memory Graph Step 3: Leak-Rate Math Step 4: Reproduce It Under a Real Limit Step 5: Find the Leaking Line Runtime Traps: JVM, Go, Node, Python The Fix and Right-Sizing the Limit Preventing the Next One: Alerts and Tests Blameless Postmortem Practice Problems Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. The Situation The orders-api service runs as 6 pods. Last week a new feature shipped: a "download my report" button. Since then: Every pod restarts roughly every 40 minutes. Users see a burst of errors each time. At night, when traffic is low, pods live for many hours. Each pod has requests.memory: 512Mi and limits.memory: 1Gi . The quick idea is "give it 2Gi". That may buy time, but if the cause is a leak, the pods will just die every 80 minutes instead. We first find out why memory grows. Two words, defined. A memory leak is memory a program keeps holding even though it will never use it again, so its memory use grows with time or traffic. OOM means "out of memory". An OOM kill is the kernel ending a process to free memory. 2. Step 1: Read the Evidence $ kubectl get pods -l app=orders-api NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE orders-api-7d9f8c6b5d-4xkzq 1/1 Running 6 (12m ago) 5h orders-api-7d9f8c6b5d-9hb2m 0/1 OOMKilled 7 (40s ago) 5h orders-api-7d9f8c6b5d-kq7wd 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 7 (2m ago) 5h ... RESTARTS counts how many times the container was restarted inside the same pod . The pod object stays; only the container is recreated. CrashLoopBackOff is not a separate error. It means "this container keeps dying, so I wait before restarting it": 10 s, then 20 s, 40 s, and so on, up to 5 minutes. The wait resets after the container runs fine for 10 minutes. $ kubectl describe pod orders-api-7d9f8c6b5d-9hb2m ... State: Running Started: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 10:41:07 +0530 Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit Code: 137 Started: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 09:58:51 +0530 Finished: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 10:41:05 +0530 Ready: True Restart Count: 7 Limits: cpu: 1 memory: 1Gi Requests: cpu: 250m memory: 512Mi What this tells us: Reason: OOMKilled means the kernel killed a process because the container went over its own memory limit (its cgroup's memory.max ). The node itself was fine. Exit Code 137 = 128 + 9. A process killed by signal number N exits with 128 + N, and 9 is SIGKILL . Started 09:58:51, Finished 10:41:05 : it lived 42 minutes. If every run lasts about the same time, memory is growing at a steady pace: a strong sign of a leak. 3. Which Kind of Kill Is It? "My pod died because of memory" can mean four different things. They have different causes and different fixes, so tell them apart first: What you see Who killed it Why Look at Reason: OOMKilled , exit 137 The kernel, inside the container's cgroup The container went over its own limits.memory The app's memory use vs its limit Pod Status: Failed , Reason: Evicted , "The node was low on resource: memory" The kubelet The node ran low; the kubelet removed pods, starting with those using the most memory above their request Node memory, other pods, requests that are too low A container dies with OOMKilled even though it was under its limit; the node log shows a system-wide OOM The kernel, for the whole node The node ran out before the kubelet could evict; the kernel picked a victim by oom_score_adj Node overcommit: sum of limits far above node RAM Exit 137 but Reason: Error , often exactly 30 s after a stop The kubelet, after the grace period The app ignored SIGTERM , so it got SIGKILL Signal handling (see PID 1 and signals ) Ours is the first row: the container's own limit.

pages.text: Scenario: A Retry Storm Takes the Service Down A production scenario: a dependency slows down, clients retry, and the service collapses. Worked math for retry amplification, a lab where success fell from 87.8% with a tight queue cap to 24.5% without one, where 8,805... Contents The Incident Words You Need How Retries Amplify Load Why It Cascades The Lab: A Slowdown at t = 2 s When the Timeout Is Shorter Than the Work The Thundering Herd The Fixes, in Order What to Look at During the Incident Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet 1. The Incident You run an API with 50 workers. Each request needs 50 ms of work from a payment service, so the chain can handle about 1,000 requests per second. Normal traffic is 400 requests per second. At 9:12 the payment service starts taking 150 ms instead of 50 ms. Its capacity drops to about 333 requests per second, a little under the 400 you are still sending. That should be a mild overflow, not an outage. Instead you see: Client timeouts (200 ms) start firing. Each timed-out request is retried three times, immediately. The payment service is now offered far more than 400 requests per second, most of them repeats of work it has already started or already finished too late. Your own queue grows. Requests spend so long in the queue that they time out after a worker has picked them up. The worker still finishes the work (abandoned work). The client has already retried, so the work is done twice, or four times, and nobody is happy. By 9:14, success looks like a floor, not a dip. This is a retry storm . The original slowdown was real. The collapse is something you helped build, in the retry policy. 2. Words You Need Timeout. How long the caller will wait for a response before giving up. If this is shorter than the work plus the queue delay, every request fails, even if the server would have gotten there eventually. Retry. Sending the same logical request again after a failure or a timeout. Amplification. How many attempts the server sees for each user request. Three retries plus the original is up to 4 if every attempt is sent. Abandoned work. The server keeps working on a request after the client has given up. The result, when it arrives, has no one waiting, and the worker was not free for a request that still had a chance. Exponential backoff. Wait 50 ms, then 100 ms, then 200 ms, and so on, between retries, instead of retrying at once. Jitter. Randomness in that wait, so that a thousand clients do not retry on the same millisecond. Retry budget. A cap on how many retries the system will start (per second, or as a fraction of live traffic). Circuit breaker. After enough recent failures, stop sending (or stop retrying) for a short time, so the dependency can recover. Load shedding. Refuse some work on purpose, early, so the work you do accept can finish inside the timeout. Idempotent. Doing the request twice has the same effect as doing it once. Safe to retry. A "charge this card" call is not idempotent unless you give it an idempotency key. Thundering herd. Many clients wake up and retry at the same time, often after a shared outage ends. 3. How Retries Amplify Load Write the amplification out before you look at a graph. Each user request may become: 1 original attempt + up to R retries If every attempt times out, offered load is (1 + R) user traffic. User traffic 400 req/s R = 3 immediate retries Offered load up to 1,600 req/s Dependency capacity after the slowdown 50 workers (1000 ms / 150 ms) = 333 req/s 1,600 into a 333-capacity service cannot recover. Even 400 into 333 was only a mild overflow. The retries are what turn a queue into a stampede. There is a second multiplier: layers . If the mobile app retries, and your API retries, and the service mesh retries, a single user action can become 4 4 4 = 64 attempts. The rule is: retry in one place , with a budget, and make the other layers fail fast or not retry at all. Intuition. A busy shop has one counter and a line. If every person wh

pages.text: Scenario: A Service Cannot Reach Its Database A real-world walkthrough: a service moved to a new Kubernetes cluster gets 'Connection timed out' talking to PostgreSQL. Reading connection errors layer by layer, DNS, TCP, firewall and route checks, ip route get... Contents The Situation Read the Error First: What Each Message Means Draw the Path Step 1: Does the Name Resolve? Step 2: Can We Open a TCP Connection? Step 3: Narrow It Down by Changing One Thing Step 4: Firewalls and Security Groups Step 5: Follow the Packet with ip route get and tcpdump The Root Cause: Overlapping Address Ranges Mitigate Now, Fix Properly Later The Next Errors: TLS and Connection Limits Blameless Postmortem Preventing It: An Address Registry and a CI Check Practice Problems Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. The Situation A shop's network in the cloud looks like this: Network A (the old one), range 10.0.0.0/16 . It holds the PostgreSQL database at 10.0.12.34 , port 5432, with the private DNS name db.internal . The old checkout servers also live here. Network B (new), range 10.1.0.0/16 . A new Kubernetes cluster runs here. Network A and Network B are joined with peering , a cloud feature that routes traffic between two private networks. Peering only works if the two ranges do not overlap, and 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/16 do not. So far, so good. On Tuesday at 11:05 IST, the team deploys the checkout service to the new cluster. Every pod crashes at start-up. The log says: psycopg.OperationalError: connection failed: connection to server at "10.0.12.34", port 5432 failed: Connection timed out Is the server running on that host and accepting TCP/IP connections? Meanwhile, the old checkout servers in Network A talk to the same database with no problem. The database dashboard shows normal CPU and normal connections. A pod is Kubernetes' smallest unit: one or more containers that share a network address. A node is a machine in the cluster that runs pods. (See Kubernetes Architecture .) 2. Read the Error First: What Each Message Means The exact wording of a connection error tells you how far the attempt got. Learning this table saves hours. Error message (typical wording) What happened on the wire Usual causes "could not translate host name", "Name or service not known", NXDOMAIN Never got an IP address. No packet was sent to the database. Typo in the name, private DNS zone not visible from this network, DNS server unreachable "Connection refused" The packet reached the machine, and it answered "no" right away (a TCP reset, RST). Nothing listening on that port, server listening only on 127.0.0.1, wrong port, a firewall set to REJECT "Connection timed out" The client sent SYN packets and nothing ever came back . A firewall that silently DROPs, a missing or wrong route, the reply going somewhere else, host down "No route to host" The local machine has no route, or a router sent back an "unreachable" message. Missing route, a firewall REJECT that uses ICMP, the target down on the local subnet (ARP fails) "Connection reset by peer" (after working a while) A connection existed, then something killed it. Idle timeout on a NAT or load balancer, server restarted, proxy limits "certificate verify failed", "SSL is required" TCP works. The TLS handshake failed. Missing CA certificate, wrong host name in the certificate, TLS turned off on one side "password authentication failed", "no pg_hba.conf entry" TCP and TLS worked. The database rejected the login. Wrong secret, the server's access rules do not allow this source address or user "sorry, too many clients already" Everything worked, but the database is out of connection slots. Too many pods too big a pool (section 11) Intuition: "refused" means you knocked and someone said "go away". "Timed out" means you knocked and heard nothing: the door might not exist, someone might be ignoring you, or the answer went to the wrong house. Our error is a timeout, so we are looking for packets that are dropped or lost, not for a stoppe

pages.text: Scenario: Debugging a Slow API End to End A full real-world walkthrough: an API gets slow after a traffic spike. Learn latency percentiles, the RED and USE methods, splitting time across network and server with curl, reading uptime and vmstat, Little's law for... Contents The Situation Words for Speed: Latency, Percentiles, Throughput Draw the Map First Two Checklists: RED and USE Step 1: Network or Server? Step 2: Is the Machine Struggling? Step 3: Where Does the Request Spend Its Time? Step 4: Little's Law and the Connection Pool Step 5: Find and Fix the Slow Query Step 6: Why It Got Worse: Retry Storms Step 7: Make It Fail Gracefully Next Time Step 8: Prove the Fix Step 9: Write a Blameless Postmortem Practice Problems Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. The Situation A shop runs an API behind a load balancer. The endpoint GET /api/orders?customer=... powers the "My orders" screen of the mobile app. Normal day: about 200 requests per second, and 99% of requests finish within 120 ms. Today a sale campaign starts at 18:00. Traffic doubles to 400 requests per second. By 18:10, some requests take over 3 seconds. Some users get 504 Gateway Timeout . The app's error rate climbs to 8%. Our job: find the cause, fix it, and make sure it does not happen again. The temptation is to guess ("the database is slow!", "add more servers!"). Guessing often works on small problems and fails on real ones. We will measure each layer instead. Intuition: debugging a slow system is like finding where a traffic jam starts. You do not stand in one spot and guess. You check the road in sections. The first section where cars are crawling, but the one after it is clear, is where the jam begins. 2. Words for Speed: Latency, Percentiles, Throughput Latency: how long one request takes, from start to finish. Throughput: how many requests are finished per second. Utilization: what fraction of time a resource (CPU, disk, a connection) is busy. Saturation: work that is waiting because the resource is already busy. A queue. Why averages lie: percentiles Here are 20 real-looking request times in milliseconds, sorted: 45 48 50 52 52 55 58 60 61 63 65 70 72 75 80 90 110 150 900 2400 The average (mean) is 4,556 / 20 = 227.8 ms . But no request actually took about 228 ms. Most were around 60 ms, and two were terrible. A percentile answers "how slow is the request that is slower than X% of all requests?" Using the simple nearest-rank rule: sort the values, and the p-th percentile is the value at position ceil(p/100 n) . Name Position (n = 20) Value Plain meaning p50 (median) ceil(0.50 20) = 10th 63 ms A typical request p90 ceil(0.90 20) = 18th 150 ms 1 in 10 is slower than this p95 ceil(0.95 20) = 19th 900 ms 1 in 20 is slower than this p99 ceil(0.99 20) = 20th 2,400 ms The "tail": 1 in 100 is slower Why care about the tail? A single screen often makes many API calls. If a page makes 10 calls and each one has a 1% chance of being slow, the chance that at least one is slow is 1 - 0.99 10 9.6% . Rare slowness per call becomes common slowness per user. That is why teams set goals on p95 or p99, not on the average. A service level objective (SLO) is such a goal written down, for example: "99% of /api/orders requests finish within 300 ms, measured over 30 days." 3. Draw the Map First Before touching any tool, draw every hop one request makes. Each arrow is a place where time can be spent or a queue can form. phone app | DNS lookup, TCP + TLS handshake (network) v load balancer ---- timeout 3 s ----+ | | v v API server 1 ... API server 4 (OS: CPU, memory, threads) | each server: 50 worker threads | each server: DB connection pool of 10 v PostgreSQL primary (database: queries, locks, disk) Write the limits on the map too: the load balancer gives up after 3 seconds (that is where the 504s come from), each server has a pool of 10 database connections, so all four servers together can hold at most 40 connections. 4. Two Checklists: RED and USE Two short checklists cover almost eve
