Suggested reading order Operating Systems Databases Computer Networks Scenarios Related tracks Suggested reading order New to these subjects? This order builds each idea on the one before it. Every page also stands on its own. Processes, Threads and CPU Scheduling : what a running program is System Calls and the Kernel Boundary : how a program asks the operating system for help Virtual Memory and Paging : how programs see memory Memory Allocation and Garbage Collection : who hands out memory, and who gives it back CPU Caches and the Memory Hierarchy : why some memory is fast and some is slow File Systems and Disk I/O : how data is saved, and when it is really safe I/O Models and Event Loops : why one slow read can stall many clients Concurrency, Synchronization and Deadlocks : what goes wrong when threads share data Normalization and Schema Design : which tables a database should have Transactions, Isolation Levels and MVCC : the same problems inside a database Indexing, B+ Trees and Query Plans : how databases find data fast SQL Joins and How the Database Executes Them : how tables are stitched back together, and how the engine does it SQL Aggregation, GROUP BY and Window Functions : turning many rows into answers Replication, Sharding and the CAP Theorem : when one database server is not enough IP Addressing, Subnetting and Routing : how packets find their way TCP Deep Dive : how bytes cross the network reliably DNS and HTTP : from a name to a web page TLS, HTTPS and Certificates : how strangers talk privately and prove who they are QUIC and HTTP/3 : a new transport over UDP, and why a lost packet should not stall every stream Load Balancing and Reverse Proxies : how traffic is spread, and why one slow server can ruin p99 Scenario: Debugging a Slow API End to End : everything above, used together Scenario: A Service Cannot Reach Its Database : a network mystery solved layer by layer Scenario: Requests Stuck on Database Locks : a lock queue, an idle transaction, and a frozen migration Scenario: Errors During Every Deploy : why releases cause 502s, measured and fixed Scenario: A Pod Keeps Getting OOMKilled : a memory leak found and fixed, from the kill to the cause Scenario: A Retry Storm Takes the Service Down : a dependency slows, clients retry, and load shedding is the fix Scenario: The Disk Is Full : deleted files that still use space, inodes, logs, and WAL Operating Systems Processes, Threads and CPU Scheduling - process states, context switches, fork/exec, threads, FCFS/SJF/SRTF/Round Robin worked by hand, Linux EEVDF and sched_ext, container CPU throttling System Calls and the Kernel Boundary - user space vs kernel space, the trap, syscall families, a lab (getpid at 66 ns vs a 0.28 ns add; writing 1 MB one byte at a time took 260 ms, one write took 0.44 ms), the vDSO, strace, N+1 I/O, seccomp I/O Models and Event Loops - blocking vs non-blocking, thread per client vs event loop, select, poll and epoll, level vs edge triggering, an event loop by hand, async/await, a lab with 200 clients (20 s vs 0.16 s), blocking the loop by mistake, backpressure Virtual Memory and Paging - address translation in hex, multi-level page tables, TLBs, page faults, FIFO/LRU/OPT traced step by step, thrashing, huge pages, OOM kills Memory Allocation and Garbage Collection - stack frames traced by hand, malloc chunks and free lists, fragmentation (freeing half the data gave back 0 KB), memory bugs, reference counting, mark and sweep by hand, generational GC, a GC pause lab, heap settings for containers CPU Caches and the Memory Hierarchy - latency numbers false-sharing slowdown and its fix, NUMA File Systems and Disk I/O - file de

pages.text: CI/CD and MLOps on Kubernetes CI/CD and MLOps from zero: pipelines, GitHub Actions, building and tagging images, GitOps with Argo CD, rolling, blue-green and canary releases, rollbacks, pipeline secrets, data and model versioning, model registries... Contents Why Pipelines Exist The Words, in Plain English CI Step by Step: a GitHub Actions Workflow CD: Getting the Image onto Kubernetes Release Strategies and Rollbacks Secrets and Permissions in Pipelines What Changes for Machine Learning (MLOps) A Model Quality Gate (Real Run) Serving Models on Kubernetes Monitoring Models: Drift and PSI Scenario: the Model That Quietly Got Worse A Real Pipeline: This Site's Own Checks Common Pitfalls Practice Problems (with Solutions) Show the code used for this scenario Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution 1. Why Pipelines Exist Imagine releasing software by hand: someone runs the tests (if they remember), builds the app on their own laptop, copies it to a server, and restarts it. Every step can go wrong, and every release is a little different. People then release rarely, so each release is big and scary. Intuition: A pipeline is a factory assembly line for code. Every change goes through the same stations in the same order: check, test, package, ship. A broken part is stopped at the station that finds it, not discovered by a customer. With a pipeline, releasing becomes boring and safe, so teams release small changes often. Small changes are easier to test and easier to undo. 2. The Words, in Plain English Word Meaning CI (continuous integration) Every change is automatically built and tested as soon as it is pushed, so problems are found within minutes. Continuous delivery Every change that passes CI is packaged and ready to release. A human presses the button. Continuous deployment Every change that passes goes to production automatically, no button. Pipeline The ordered list of automated steps. Artifact The thing the pipeline produces and ships, for example a container image or a model file. Registry A store for artifacts. Container registries hold images (GHCR, Docker Hub, ECR). Model registries hold models. Environment A place the app runs: dev, staging (a production copy for final checks), production. GitOps Git holds the desired state of the cluster. A tool inside the cluster keeps the cluster matching Git. Rollback Going back to the previous working version. developer pushes code | v +------------- CI -------------+ +----------- CD ------------+ | lint - unit tests - build | -- | update deploy repo | | image - scan - push image | | - Argo CD syncs cluster | +------------------------------+ | - canary - full rollout | | any step fails = stop +---------------------------+ v | developer gets a red X on the PR v monitoring, alerts, rollback 3. CI Step by Step: a GitHub Actions Workflow GitHub Actions runs pipelines defined in YAML files inside your repository, in the folder .github/workflows/ . The parts: on: which events start it (a pull request, a push to main, a schedule). jobs: groups of steps. Jobs run in parallel unless one needs another. runs-on: the kind of machine (runner) the job uses. steps: either uses: (a ready-made action, like checking out the code) or run: (a shell command). Here is a complete workflow for a Python API that also ships a model. It runs tests on every pull request, runs a model quality gate (section 8), and on a push to main builds an image and pushes it to the GitHub container registry: name: ci on: pull_request: push: branches: [main] permissions: contents: read packages: write env: IMAGE: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/api jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: "3.12" cache: pip - run: pip install -r requirements.txt - run: ruff check . - run: pytest -q model-gate: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: "3.12" - run: pip insta

pages.text: Infrastructure as Code Infrastructure as Code from zero: desired state vs actual state, why console clicks drift, a runnable reconciler that planned 2 updates and 1 delete to fix a leaked firewall rule, Terraform plan/apply/state, modules... Contents The Problem with Clicking in a Console Words You Need Imperative vs Declarative The Lab: A Tiny Reconciler Terraform: Plan, Apply, State The State File Is Precious Modules, Workspaces, and Blast Radius Secrets Do Not Belong in the File Terraform, Pulumi, Ansible, and Kubernetes Plan on the Pull Request, Apply on Merge Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet 1. The Problem with Clicking in a Console A team has a database that should only accept connections from the web subnet, 10.0.1.0/24 , on port 5432. On Monday someone debugs a laptop connection and, in the cloud console, adds a rule: allow 0.0.0.0/0 on 5432. The bug is fixed. The rule stays. Nobody reviews it, because there is no diff. Three months later a scan finds a database on the public internet. The same story happens in quieter ways: Two environments, "staging" and "production," started the same and slowly stopped matching, because each change was clicked only in one of them. A machine was created by hand, never recorded, and was missed by a backup policy. After an incident, nobody can answer "what did we change last Thursday?" Infrastructure as code treats the desired shape of the system as a set of files. A tool compares that shape to what really exists, shows a plan (create, update, delete), and only then applies it. The files go through the same review as application code. Intuition. A console is a conversation you cannot replay. A file is a recipe. If the cake comes out wrong, you can read the recipe, see the last change, and bake it again the same way in another kitchen. 2. Words You Need Desired state. What you said you want: three web servers on image app:1.4 , a database, a tight firewall. Actual state. What exists right now in the cloud or in the cluster. Drift. The two states do not match. Someone clicked, a process failed halfway, or an auto-scaler changed a count. Reconcile. Compute the difference and take the actions that make actual state match desired state. Plan. A preview of those actions, without doing them yet. Apply. Carry out the plan. State file. The tool's own record of what it created and which real objects map to which resources in the files. Terraform's terraform.tfstate is the usual example. Idempotent apply. Running apply twice with no changes the second time. The second plan is empty. Provider. The plugin that talks to a particular API (one cloud, DNS, Kubernetes, and so on). 3. Imperative vs Declarative An imperative script says how to do the work, step by step: create_vpc() create_subnet() create_vm(count=3) # if you run this again, it may try to create a second VPC # and fail, or worse, create a duplicate A declarative file says what you want, and leaves the how to the tool: web: { count: 3, image: "app:1.4" } If three servers already exist with that image, the tool does nothing. If two exist, it creates one. If the image is old, it updates them. Kubernetes manifests, Terraform configurations, and the lab below are declarative. Ansible can be used either way; many playbooks are a mix (declarative modules called in an imperative order). Declarative does not mean "no danger." A file that says count: 0 will delete everything that used to be there. The plan is how you see that before it happens. 4. The Lab: A Tiny Reconciler You do not need a cloud account to see the idea. We wrote a small Python program that treats dictionaries as "the infrastructure." Desired state is the file you would keep in git. Actual state is what we found after a week of console clicks. desired = { "vpc": {"cidr": "10.0.0.0/16"}, "subnet-public": {"cidr": "10.0.1.0/24", "in": "vpc"}, "subnet-private": {"cidr": "10.0.2.0/24", "in": "vpc"}, "web": {"count": 3, "image": "app:1.4", "subnet": "subnet-public", "cpu_m

Contents Why These Tools Exist The Words, in Plain English What Makes a Run Reproducible Experiment Tracking (Real MLflow Run) The Model Registry: Versions and Aliases Promotion and Rollback, Step by Step Training-Serving Skew Point-in-Time Joins, by Hand Feature Stores: Offline and Online Scenario: the Fraud Model That Missed Half the Fraud How It Fits on Kubernetes Common Pitfalls Practice Problems (with Solutions) Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution 1. Why These Tools Exist Normal software has one moving part: code. Git tracks it. An ML system has three moving parts: code , data , and the model (the file that training produces). Git alone tracks only the first. code (git) ─┐ data ─┼─► training run ─► model file ─► registry ─► serving settings ─┘ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ experiment tracking: "version 7 is features at request params, metrics, files champion" time must match the features used in training (feature store) Intuition. A lab scientist keeps a notebook: what they mixed, how much, at what temperature, and what happened. Without it, a great result cannot be repeated. Experiment tracking is that notebook. The model registry is the shelf of labelled, approved samples. The feature store makes sure the kitchen uses the same recipe as the lab. 2. The Words, in Plain English Word Meaning Run One training attempt, with its settings, results and output files. Experiment A named group of runs that try to solve the same problem. Parameter (param) A setting you chose for a run, like learning rate or tree depth. Metric A number that measures the result, like validation AUC. Artifact A file a run produced: the model, a plot, a list of features. Lineage The chain that says where something came from: model version 7 came from run X, which used commit Y and data snapshot Z. Registered model / version A named model in the registry ("fraud-detector"), with numbered versions 1, 2, 3... Alias A movable name tag pointing at one version, like champion or challenger . Feature An input number for the model, like "average spend in the last 30 days". Entity The thing a feature describes: a user, a card, a product. Training-serving skew A feature has a different value (or meaning) in production than it had in training. Point-in-time join Attaching to each training example the feature values as they were at that moment , not as they are today. 3. What Makes a Run Reproducible To train the same model again, you need five things. Missing any one is a common reason a "great model from last month" cannot be rebuilt. Ingredient How to pin it Example Code Git commit hash 3f2a9c1 Data A snapshot path plus a content hash, or a data versioning tool (DVC, lakeFS, table snapshots) s3://ml/fraud/2026-11-01/ , sha256 9b1e... Settings All params logged, config file saved as an artifact C=1.0 , max_iter=1000 Environment A lock file of exact library versions, or a container image digest scikit-learn==1.9.1 , image @sha256:... Randomness Fixed seeds for splits, initialisation and sampling random_state=0 Even then, GPU training can differ in the last digits from run to run (the order of floating-point additions changes). Aim for "same metrics within noise", not "same bytes". A content hash is one line of Python: import hashlib digest = hashlib.sha256(open("train.parquet", "rb").read()).hexdigest() # log it with the run, e.g. mlflow.set_tag("data_sha256", digest) If anyone changes one byte of the file, the hash changes, so you can prove two runs used the same data. 4. pages.text: How Containers Really Work Containers from zero, proven with real commands: a container is a normal Linux process plus namespaces (what it can see), cgroups (what it can use), and a layered root filesystem (overlayfs). Hands-on labs with unshare... Contents The Big Idea in One Picture Namespaces: What a Process Can See Lab: Your First Namespaces with unshare Network Namespaces, veth Pairs, and Bridges PID 1 and Signals: Why Containers Ignore Ctrl+C cgroups: What a Process Can Use Lab: Memory, CPU, and Process Limits The Root Filesystem: Layers and overlayfs An Image, Pulled Apart by Hand Who Does What: docker, containerd, runc, kubelet Security Layers and Their Limits Capstone: A Container from Scratch Practice Problems Common Pitfalls Cheat Sheet 1. The Big Idea in One Picture When you run docker run nginx , the kernel starts a normal process, just like when you type nginx in a terminal. The difference is that the process is started inside a box made of three kernel features: +-----------------------------------------------+ | one ordinary process | | (e.g. nginx) | +-----------------------------------------------+ | | | NAMESPACES | CGROUPS | ROOT FILESYSTEM "what can I see?" "how much can I use?" "which files are mine?" own PIDs, own memory.max = 512M image layers stacked network, own cpu.max = 1 CPU with overlayfs, plus a hostname, own pids.max = 100 thin writable layer mounts, users + security filters: capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux, user namespaces A namespace gives a process its own private copy of one kind of system resource (process IDs, network, hostname, mounts...). Other processes outside it see their own copy. A cgroup (control group) is a group of processes that the kernel counts and limits together: memory, CPU time, number of processes, disk I/O. The root filesystem is the set of files the process sees at / . For a container, it comes from the image, stacked with overlayfs . Intuition: a virtual machine is a separate house with its own foundation (its own kernel). A container is a room in a shared house: it has its own door, its own furniture, and a meter on its power use, but it shares the foundation, the pipes, and the wiring (the host kernel) with every other room. Because a container is just a process, you can see it from the host. On a Docker host, ps aux | grep nginx shows the container's nginx with a normal host PID. That one fact explains a lot: containers start in milliseconds (no OS to boot), they are as fast as normal processes, and a kernel bug can affect all of them at once. 2. Namespaces: What a Process Can See Linux has eight kinds of namespaces. A container usually gets a new one of each kind except, sometimes, user and time. Namespace Isolates What the container sees mnt (mount) The list of mounted filesystems Its own / , its own /proc , its volumes pid Process ID numbers Its first process is PID 1; host processes are invisible net Network interfaces, IPs, routes, ports, firewall rules Its own eth0 and lo ; port 80 is free even if the host uses it uts Hostname Its own hostname (Docker uses the container ID) ipc Shared memory and message queues Its own /dev/shm segments user User and group IDs Can be "root" (UID 0) inside while being an unprivileged UID like 100000 on the host cgroup The view of the cgroup tree Its own cgroup looks like the root time Boot and monotonic clocks Can have its own uptime (rarely used) Every process points at one namespace of each kind. You can see them as links in /proc : $ ls -l /proc/self/ns lrwxrwxrwx 1 box box 0 Nov 22 14:20 cgroup - cgroup:[4026531835] lrwxrwxrwx 1 box box 0 Nov 22 14:20 ipc - ipc:[4026532324] lrwxrwxrwx 1 box box 0 Nov 22 14:20 mnt - mnt:[4026532292] lrwxrwxrwx 1 box box 0 Nov 22 14:20 net - net:[4026531840] lrwxrwxrwx 1 box box 0 Nov 22 14:20 pid - pid:[4026532325] lrwxrwxrwx 1 box box 0 Nov 22 14:20 uts - uts:[4026532323] ... The number in brackets is the namespace's ID. Two processes with the same number for net share one network st

pages.text: Advanced Docker Advanced Docker: multi-stage builds, BuildKit, image security, registries, CI/CD integration, rootless mode, and cgroup resource limits. Contents Multi-Stage Builds Deep Dive BuildKit Features Image Security & Scanning Container Registries Docker in CI/CD Rootless Docker Resource Limits & cgroups Cheat Sheet 1. Multi-Stage Builds Deep Dive A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM statements in one Dockerfile. Each stage is an independent build environment; you copy only the artifacts you need into the final image. The result: smaller images, no compiler toolchains in production, and faster deploys. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Stage: builder Stage: production │ │ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │ │ │ golang:1.22 │ │ distroless/base │ │ │ │ compile binary │───▶│ COPY binary only │ final ~15 MB │ │ │ (500 MB tools) │ │ no shell, no gcc │ │ │ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │ │ intermediate layers discarded - not in final image │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Go application (distroless) # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /src COPY go.mod go.sum ./ RUN go mod download COPY . . RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o /app/server ./cmd/server FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot COPY --from=builder /app/server /server USER nonroot:nonroot EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] Node.js application FROM node:20-alpine AS deps WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev FROM node:20-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build FROM node:20-alpine AS production WORKDIR /app ENV NODE_ENV=production COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist COPY package.json ./ USER node EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"] Named stages and cross-stage copies FROM alpine AS base RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates FROM base AS tools RUN apk add --no-cache curl jq FROM base AS app COPY --from=tools /usr/bin/curl /usr/bin/curl # copy single binary COPY --from=tools /usr/lib/libjq.so* /usr/lib/ COPY ./app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app/run.sh"] Build a specific stage # Build only the builder stage (for debugging compile issues) docker build --target builder -t myapp:builder . # Build production image (default: last stage) docker build -t myapp:2.1.0 . Layer caching: Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changing. Copy dependency manifests and run npm ci / go mod download before copying source code so dependency layers stay cached across builds. 2. BuildKit Features BuildKit is the modern Docker build engine (default since Docker 23.0). It provides parallel stage execution, advanced caching, secrets during build, SSH agent forwarding, and improved Dockerfile frontend features. Enable BuildKit # Enabled by default in recent Docker Desktop and Engine export DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 # Explicit builder instance (Buildx) docker buildx create --name mybuilder --use docker buildx inspect --bootstrap Cache mounts (speed up package installs) # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM node:20-alpine AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \ npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build FROM golang:1.22 AS builder RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \ --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \ go build -o /app/server . Build secrets (never in image layers) # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 FROM alpine RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \ NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token) && \ echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}" > .npmrc && \ npm ci && rm .npmrc # Build with secret file docker build --secret id=npm_token,src=./.npm_token . SSH mount (private Git repos) FROM alpine RUN apk add --no-cache git openssh-client RUN --mount=type=ssh \ mkdir -p ~/.ssh && ssh-keyscan github.com >> ~/.s

pages.text: Docker Compose Docker Compose: multi-service apps, compose files, networking, volumes, secrets, health checks, overrides, CLI, and production patterns. Contents What is Docker Compose? The Compose File Services in Depth Networking Volumes Environment & Secrets Health Checks & Dependencies Override Files Compose CLI Production Patterns Cheat Sheet 1. What is Docker Compose? Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications. You describe your stack in a compose.yaml file - services, networks, volumes, environment variables - and Compose creates and wires everything together with a single command. Compose is ideal for: Local development - spin up an API, database, cache, and message broker together. Integration testing - reproducible test environments in CI pipelines. Small deployments - single-host production stacks (with caveats; see Production Patterns). Demos and onboarding - one command to run the entire application. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ docker compose up │ │ │ │ │ ├── creates network: myapp_default │ │ ├── creates volume: myapp_postgres_data │ │ ├── starts container: myapp-postgres-1 │ │ ├── starts container: myapp-redis-1 │ │ └── starts container: myapp-api-1 (depends on above) │ │ │ │ │ └── DNS: api, postgres, redis resolve on network │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Compose v2: Use docker compose (space, not hyphen). The legacy standalone docker-compose Python tool is deprecated. Compose v2 is a Go-based Docker CLI plugin integrated with Buildx and Docker contexts. Quick start # Project layout myapp/ ├── compose.yaml ├── api/ │ └── Dockerfile └── .env # Start everything in the foreground docker compose up # Start detached, rebuild images docker compose up -d --build # Tear down containers, networks, and named volumes docker compose down -v 2. The Compose File Modern Compose files follow the Compose Specification (compose-spec.io). The top-level version field is no longer required - Compose v2 infers the schema automatically. Top-level keys Key Purpose services Container definitions (required) networks Custom bridge/overlay networks volumes Named or external volume declarations secrets File-based secrets mounted into containers configs Non-sensitive config files (Swarm-oriented, limited in standalone) name Override the default project name (directory name) Minimal compose.yaml name: myapp services: web: image: nginx:1.27-alpine ports: - "8080:80" volumes: - ./html:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro api: build: context: ./api dockerfile: Dockerfile ports: - "3000:3000" environment: DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/appdb depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy db: image: postgres:16-alpine environment: POSTGRES_USER: app POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret POSTGRES_DB: appdb volumes: - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d appdb"] interval: 5s timeout: 3s retries: 5 volumes: postgres_data: Build context options services: api: build: context: . # directory sent to docker build dockerfile: docker/api.Dockerfile target: production # multi-stage build target args: NODE_VERSION: "20" cache_from: - myregistry/api:cache labels: org.opencontainers.image.source: https://github.com/org/repo image: myregistry/api:${TAG:-latest} # tag the built image 3. Services in Depth Each entry under services maps to one or more containers (replicas with deploy.replicas in Swarm mode; standalone Compose runs one container per service). Image vs build Approach When to use image: nginx:1.27 Pull a pre-built image from a registry build: ./api Build locally from a Dockerfile Both Build locally and tag with image for push/reuse Common service options services: worker: image: myapp/worker:2.1.0 restart: unless-stopped # no | always | on-failure | unless-stopped user: "1000:1000" # run as non-root working_dir: /app command: ["node", "worker.js"] # override image CMD entrypoint: ["/entry

pages.description: Docker fundamentals: containers vs VMs, architecture, images and layers, Dockerfile, CLI, networking, volumes, and best practices.
pages.text: Docker Fundamentals Docker fundamentals: containers vs VMs, architecture, images and layers, Dockerfile, CLI, networking, volumes, and best practices. Contents Containers vs Virtual Machines Docker Architecture Images & Layers Dockerfile Docker CLI Networking Volumes & Storage Best Practices Cheat Sheet 1. Containers vs Virtual Machines A virtual machine (VM) runs a full guest operating system on a hypervisor. Each VM has its own kernel, drivers, and userland. VMs are strong isolation boundaries but heavy: gigabytes of disk, seconds to minutes to boot, and significant CPU overhead for the hypervisor. A container is an isolated process (or process tree) on the host kernel. Linux kernel features provide the isolation: Namespaces control what a process can see : PID, network, mounts, hostname, IPC, and user ID mappings. cgroups (control groups) limit what a process can consume : CPU, memory, block I/O, and network bandwidth. Capabilities and seccomp restrict which privileged syscalls a container may invoke. Want to see these pieces with your own eyes? How Containers Really Work builds each one by hand with unshare , cgroup files, and overlayfs, then assembles a container without Docker. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ VM model │ │ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ │ │ Guest OS │ │ Guest OS │ │ Guest OS │ each with own kernel │ │ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ │ │ └─────────────┴─────────────┘ │ │ Hypervisor (KVM, Hyper-V) │ │ Host OS + hardware │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Container model │ │ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ │ │ App proc │ │ App proc │ │ App proc │ share host kernel │ │ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ │ │ └─────────────┴─────────────┘ │ │ containerd + runc (namespaces + cgroups) │ │ Host OS + hardware │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Aspect VM Container Isolation Separate kernel per VM Shared kernel, namespace boundaries Startup Seconds to minutes Milliseconds Size GBs (full OS) MBs (app + minimal runtime) Density Tens per host Hundreds per host Best for Multi-tenant, mixed OS, strong isolation Microservices, CI/CD, cloud-native apps When to choose which: Use VMs when you need a different OS, kernel version, or hardware-level isolation. Use containers when you want fast, dense, reproducible application packaging on a shared Linux (or Windows container) host. 2. Docker Architecture Docker follows a client-server model. The CLI sends API requests; the daemon manages resources; the runtime actually starts processes. docker CLI dockerd (daemon) container runtime ────────── ──────────────── ───────────────── docker build ──REST──▶ manages images, containerd docker run containers, └── runc (OCI runtime) docker ps networks, volumes │ │ ▼ └── talks to registry Linux namespaces (Docker Hub, ECR, + cgroups GHCR, private) Key components docker - the client CLI. Sends commands to the daemon via Unix socket ( /var/run/docker.sock on Linux) or TCP. dockerd - the daemon. Builds images, pulls/pushes to registries, creates networks and volumes, orchestrates container lifecycle. containerd - industry-standard container runtime. Manages image transfer, container execution, and snapshots. runc - OCI-compliant low-level runtime that creates the container process with namespaces and cgroups. Registry - stores and distributes images (Docker Hub, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, GitHub Container Registry). Container lifecycle docker create # allocate filesystem + config, do not start docker start # run the main process docker stop # SIGTERM, grace period (default 10s), then SIGKILL docker rm # delete container and writable layer docker run # create + start in one step A stopped container retains its writable layer until removed. Image layers are never modified by running containers. 3. Images and Layers A Docker image i

pages.description: Kubernetes architecture: control plane, worker nodes, etcd, API server, scheduler, controllers, kubelet, kube-proxy, kubectl, and reconciliation.
pages.text: Kubernetes Architecture Kubernetes architecture: control plane, worker nodes, etcd, API server, scheduler, controllers, kubelet, kube-proxy, kubectl, and reconciliation. Contents Why Kubernetes? Cluster Overview Control Plane Components Worker Node Components kubectl Mastery API Resources & Objects The Reconciliation Loop Cluster Setup Options Cheat Sheet 1. Why Kubernetes? Running containers on a single host is easy. Running hundreds of microservices across dozens of machines is not. Kubernetes (K8s) solves the operational problems of distributed container orchestration: Scheduling - place containers on nodes with available CPU, memory, and affinity rules. Self-healing - restart failed containers, replace unhealthy Pods, reschedule when nodes die. Scaling - scale replicas up or down manually or automatically (HPA). Service discovery and load balancing - stable DNS names and virtual IPs for ephemeral Pods. Declarative config - describe desired state in YAML; controllers reconcile reality to match. Rolling updates and rollbacks - zero-downtime deploys with version history. Secrets and config management - inject configuration without baking it into images. Storage orchestration - attach cloud or network storage to any Pod. Without K8s With K8s SSH into servers, run docker run manually Apply a Deployment; scheduler places Pods automatically Custom scripts for health checks and restarts kubelet + controllers restart and replace failed Pods Hard-coded IPs or external load balancers per service ClusterIP Services with built-in DNS Manual blue/green deploys RollingUpdate strategy with kubectl rollout undo Kubernetes is not a PaaS. It provides primitives (Pods, Services, Deployments) that you compose into a platform. You still choose ingress, CI/CD, observability, and policy tooling on top. 2. Cluster Overview A Kubernetes cluster consists of at least one control plane and one or more worker nodes . The control plane makes global decisions (scheduling, API, state storage). Worker nodes run your workloads. Kubernetes cluster architecture kubectl talks to the API server. The scheduler and controller manager watch the API server. Only the API server reads and writes etcd. On each worker node the kubelet watches the API server and starts pods through the container runtime. kube-proxy programs Service rules. CONTROL PLANE WORKER NODE 1 WORKER NODE 2 kubectl / CI kube-scheduler picks a node for each pod controller-manager reconcile loops kube-apiserver the only front door etcd cluster state (key-value) kube-proxy Service rules kubelet node agent Pods your containers containerd runtime + CNI kube-proxy Service rules kubelet node agent Pods your containers containerd runtime + CNI HTTPS + auth watch pods, report status Everything goes through the API server. Components watch it for changes and write their results back. High-availability control planes run multiple API server instances behind a load balancer, with etcd deployed as a 3- or 5-node quorum cluster. Worker nodes are cattle - add or remove them without manual reconfiguration. Namespaces Logical partitions inside a cluster. Resources in different namespaces can share the same physical nodes but are isolated by RBAC and naming. kubectl get namespaces # default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease - plus your own kubectl create namespace production kubectl get pods -n production 3. Control Plane Components Every control plane component is a process (or Pod in managed clusters) that watches or writes cluster state through the API server . etcd is the sole source of truth for persisted state. API Server ( kube-apiserver ) The front door to the cluster. All clients (kubectl, kubelet, controllers, scheduler) communicate exclusively via the REST API. It validates requests, applies admission webhooks, persists objects to etcd, and serves watch streams. Authenticates requests (certs, bearer tokens, OIDC) Authorizes via RBAC, Node, or webhook modes Admits or mutates objects through admis

pages.text: Autoscaling, Probes & Rollouts Keeping a Kubernetes app healthy while traffic and code change: requests as the base of everything, startup, readiness and liveness probes with timing math, rolling updates with maxSurge and maxUnavailable worked step... Contents The Big Picture The Words, in Plain English Requests: the Number Everything Depends On Probes: Startup, Readiness, Liveness Rolling Updates, Step by Step How a Pod Shuts Down The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) Scaling Speed: Behavior and Stabilization The Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) Adding Machines: Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter PodDisruptionBudgets Putting It Together: a Traffic Spike, Minute by Minute The Full Manifests (Validated) Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet 1. The Big Picture traffic goes up new release │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────── HPA: more pods ◄── metrics Deployment: rolling update │ │ │ │ pods are Pending (no room) new pods must pass the │ ▼ readiness probe before │ Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter: they get traffic │ add a machine (node) │ │ ▼ ▼ └────► pods start ─► startup probe ─► readiness probe ─► Service sends traffic liveness probe ─► restart if stuck Each tool answers one question: Tool Question it answers What it changes Startup probe Has the app finished starting? Holds off the other probes until it has Readiness probe Should this pod get traffic right now? Adds or removes the pod from the Service Liveness probe Is the app stuck and needs a restart? Restarts the container Rolling update How do we replace old pods with new ones safely? Creates and deletes pods in steps HPA How many pods do we need? The replica count VPA How much CPU and memory should each pod ask for? The pod's requests Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter Do we have enough machines? The number of nodes PodDisruptionBudget How many pods may be taken down on purpose at once? Blocks evictions that would go below the limit 2. The Words, in Plain English Word Meaning Pod One running copy of your app (one or more containers sharing an IP address). Node A machine that runs pods. Replica One of several identical pods. "4 replicas" means 4 copies. Deployment The object that says "keep N replicas of this pod template running" and manages updates. Service / endpoints A stable address that spreads traffic over the ready pods. The list of ready pod IPs behind it is called its endpoints. Probe A check the kubelet (the agent on each node) runs against a container: an HTTP request, a TCP connect, a command, or a gRPC health check. Pending A pod that the scheduler could not place on any node yet, usually because no node has enough free CPU or memory. Eviction Removing a pod from a node on purpose, for example to empty the node for maintenance. Millicores (m) Thousandths of a CPU core. 500m = half a core. 3. Requests: the Number Everything Depends On Every container can say how much CPU and memory it needs, its request (see Resource Requests and Limits ). Three tools on this page read that number: The scheduler only places a pod on a node with that much unclaimed room. The HPA measures CPU as a percentage of the request . A pod with request 500m that uses 300m is at 60% utilization. The Cluster Autoscaler adds a node when pods do not fit by request, and removes nodes whose pods ask for little. Intuition. Requests are a reservation , like booking seats in a restaurant. The scheduler counts booked seats, not people actually eating. If you book too few seats, the HPA thinks every pod is overloaded. If you book too many, nodes look full while the CPUs sit idle, and you pay for machines you do not use. Without a CPU request, the HPA cannot compute a CPU percentage at all, and it reports an error instead of scaling. 4. Probes: Startup, Readiness, Liveness The kubelet runs each probe every periodSeconds . A probe "fails" if the HTTP status is not 200-399, the TCP connect fails, the command exits non-zero, or there is no answer within timeoutSeconds . After failureThreshold failures in a row, the probe'

pages.text: Config, Secrets & Security Kubernetes ConfigMaps, Secrets, RBAC, ServiceAccounts, Pod Security Standards, OPA Gatekeeper, and security hardening. Contents ConfigMaps Secrets ServiceAccounts RBAC Pod Security Standards Admission Controllers & OPA Pod Hardening Checklist Cheat Sheet 1. ConfigMaps ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs. They can be mounted as files or injected as environment variables. apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: app-config namespace: production data: APP_ENV: production LOG_LEVEL: info config.yaml: | server: port: 8080 timeout: 30s database: pool_size: 20 Mount as environment variables env: - name: APP_ENV valueFrom: configMapKeyRef: name: app-config key: APP_ENV envFrom: - configMapRef: name: app-config # all keys become env vars Mount as files volumeMounts: - name: config mountPath: /etc/app/config.yaml subPath: config.yaml readOnly: true volumes: - name: config configMap: name: app-config Hot reload: ConfigMap updates do not automatically restart Pods. Use a sidecar (Reloader, Stakater Reloader) or roll out a new Deployment revision to pick up changes. 2. Secrets Secrets store sensitive data (passwords, tokens, TLS certs). They are base64-encoded in etcd - not encrypted by default . Enable encryption at rest for production. apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-credentials type: Opaque stringData: # preferred - Kubernetes encodes to base64 for you DB_USER: appuser DB_PASSWORD: s3cr3tP@ss DB_HOST: postgres.production.svc.cluster.local Secret types Type Use Opaque Arbitrary user-defined data kubernetes.io/tls TLS cert + key ( tls.crt , tls.key ) kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Docker registry credentials kubernetes.io/service-account-token Legacy SA token (avoid; use TokenRequest API) Encryption at rest # /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1 kind: EncryptionConfiguration resources: - resources: - secrets providers: - aescbc: keys: - name: key1 secret: base64-encoded-32-byte-key - identity: {} # fallback for unencrypted secrets External secret management For production, prefer external secret stores integrated via: External Secrets Operator - syncs AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault into K8s Secrets Sealed Secrets - encrypt Secrets for safe storage in Git HashiCorp Vault - inject secrets via Vault Agent sidecar or CSI driver # External Secrets Operator example apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1 kind: ExternalSecret metadata: name: db-credentials spec: refreshInterval: 1h secretStoreRef: name: aws-secrets-manager kind: ClusterSecretStore target: name: db-credentials data: - secretKey: DB_PASSWORD remoteRef: key: production/db property: password 3. ServiceAccounts Every Pod runs as a ServiceAccount . It provides an identity for in-cluster API access and (optionally) cloud IAM via workload identity. apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: api-sa namespace: production annotations: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/api-pod-role spec: serviceAccountName: api-sa automountServiceAccountToken: false # disable if Pod doesn't need K8s API access Default ServiceAccount: Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount. Never run production workloads with it - create dedicated ServiceAccounts with minimal permissions. 4. pages.text: GPU Scheduling on Kubernetes Running GPU workloads on Kubernetes from zero: device plugins, the NVIDIA GPU Operator, requesting GPUs, taints and node labels, sharing GPUs with time-slicing, MPS and MIG, Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), gang... Contents Why GPUs Are Different from CPU and Memory Device Plugins: How Kubernetes Learns About GPUs The NVIDIA GPU Operator Requesting a GPU in a Pod Putting GPU Pods on the Right Nodes Sharing GPUs: Time-Slicing, MPS, and MIG Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) Distributed Training and Gang Scheduling Serving an LLM: a Complete Deployment Autoscaling and Cost Monitoring GPUs Scenario: My GPU Pod Is Stuck in Pending Common Pitfalls 1. Why GPUs Are Different from CPU and Memory Kubernetes was built around CPU and memory. Those are easy: the kubelet reads them from the operating system, and the Linux kernel can divide them finely (CPU shares, memory limits). GPUs break those assumptions: Kubernetes does not know they exist. The kubelet cannot discover GPUs by itself. A vendor plugin must tell it. They are whole devices. You cannot ask for "0.3 of a GPU" the way you ask for 300m CPU. GPU counts are integers. No overcommit. A GPU given to one container is not handed to another (unless you explicitly set up sharing, section 6). Extra software is needed on the node: a kernel driver, a container runtime hook that mounts the device files and driver libraries into containers, and the CUDA libraries in the image. They are expensive. An idle H100 costs real money every hour. Good scheduling is about cost as much as correctness. Intuition: CPU and memory are like water from a tap: you can take any amount. GPUs are like rental cars: you take a whole car, someone has to register the cars with the rental office first (device plugin), and you might want a specific model (node labels). 2. Device Plugins: How Kubernetes Learns About GPUs The device plugin framework is how hardware vendors teach the kubelet about special devices without changing Kubernetes code. Step by step The vendor's device plugin runs on each GPU node, usually as a DaemonSet. It finds the GPUs (for NVIDIA, through the driver's management library) and registers with the kubelet over a gRPC Unix socket in /var/lib/kubelet/device-plugins/ . It advertises an extended resource name and count, for example nvidia.com/gpu: 8 , and reports device health. The kubelet adds this to the node's status.capacity and status.allocatable . Now the scheduler can see it. When a Pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 is scheduled to the node, the kubelet asks the plugin to allocate a specific device. The plugin returns what the container needs: device files, environment variables (which GPU IDs are visible), and mounts. The container runtime (with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit) starts the container with only that GPU visible. $ kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GPUS:.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu NAME GPUS cpu-node-1 none gpu-node-1 8 gpu-node-2 8 3. The NVIDIA GPU Operator Installing and upgrading drivers, toolkit, and plugin by hand on every node is error-prone. The NVIDIA GPU Operator (installed with Helm) manages all of it as containers: Component Job Driver container Installs the kernel driver on the node (can be skipped if the node image already has it, as on many managed clouds) Container Toolkit Configures containerd/CRI-O so containers can access GPUs Device plugin Advertises nvidia.com/gpu (section 2) GPU Feature Discovery (GFD) Adds node labels such as GPU product, memory, count, and MIG capability DCGM exporter Exposes GPU metrics to Prometheus MIG manager Applies MIG partition layouts from a node label helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia and and helm repo update helm install gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator -n gpu-operator --create-namespace # a few minutes later kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator kubectl get node gpu-node-1 --show-labels | tr ',' '\n' | grep nvidia.com/gpu Typical GFD labels: nvidia.com/

pages.description: Helm charts, releases, values, Prometheus, Grafana, logging, tracing, and resource quotas for Kubernetes.
pages.text: Helm & Observability Helm charts, releases, values, Prometheus, Grafana, logging, tracing, and resource quotas for Kubernetes. Contents Helm Basics Chart Anatomy Templates & Values Helm Workflow Prometheus & Metrics Grafana Dashboards Logging Distributed Tracing Resource Quotas & Limits Cheat Sheet 1. Helm Basics Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a collection of templated YAML manifests. A release is a deployed instance of a chart in a cluster. # Install Helm curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash # Add a chart repository helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts helm repo update # Search charts helm search repo nginx helm search hub postgres Helm 3 vs Helm 2: Helm 3 has no Tiller (in-cluster server). Releases are stored as Secrets in the release namespace. Always use Helm 3. 2. Chart Anatomy mychart/ ├── Chart.yaml # chart metadata (name, version, dependencies) ├── values.yaml # default configuration values ├── charts/ # dependent charts (subcharts) ├── templates/ # Kubernetes manifest templates │ ├── deployment.yaml │ ├── service.yaml │ ├── ingress.yaml │ ├── _helpers.tpl # reusable template functions │ └── NOTES.txt # post-install instructions └── .helmignore Chart.yaml apiVersion: v2 name: myapp description: My application Helm chart type: application version: 1.2.0 # chart version appVersion: "2.3.1" # application version dependencies: - name: postgresql version: "12.x.x" repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami condition: postgresql.enabled 3. Templates and Values Helm uses Go templates with Sprig functions. Values from values.yaml (and overrides) are injected into templates. values.yaml replicaCount: 3 image: repository: mycompany/api tag: "2.3.1" pullPolicy: IfNotPresent service: type: ClusterIP port: 80 ingress: enabled: true host: api.example.com tls: true resources: requests: cpu: 100m memory: 128Mi limits: cpu: 500m memory: 512Mi autoscaling: enabled: true minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 10 targetCPUUtilization: 70 deployment.yaml template apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: {{ include "myapp.fullname" . }} labels: {{- include "myapp.labels" . | nindent 4 }} spec: {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }} replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }} {{- end }} selector: matchLabels: {{- include "myapp.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }} template: metadata: labels: {{- include "myapp.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }} spec: containers: - name: {{ .Chart.Name }} image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}" imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }} ports: - containerPort: 8080 resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }} livenessProbe: httpGet: path: /health port: 8080 readinessProbe: httpGet: path: /ready port: 8080 Common template functions {{ .Values.replicaCount }} # access value {{ .Release.Name }} # release name {{ .Release.Namespace }} # target namespace {{ include "myapp.fullname" . }} # call named template {{ .Values.ingress.enabled | ternary "enabled" "disabled" }} {{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }} # conditional block {{- range .Values.env }} # loop {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }} # indent YAML block 4. Helm Workflow # Install a release helm install my-api bitnami/nginx \ --namespace production \ --create-namespace \ --set replicaCount=3 \ --set service.type=LoadBalancer # Install with values file helm install my-api ./mychart -f values-prod.yaml -f values-secrets.yaml # Upgrade (deploy new version) helm upgrade my-api ./mychart --set image.tag=2.4.0 # Upgrade or install (idempotent) helm upgrade --install my-api ./mychart -f values-prod.yaml # Rollback helm rollback my-api 2 # rollback to revision 2 helm history my-api # Uninstall helm uninstall my-api -n production # Dry-run (render templates without applying) helm template my-api ./mychart -f values-prod.yaml helm install my-api ./mychart --

pages.text: Kubernetes Networking & Services Kubernetes networking: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, Ingress, DNS, Network Policies, CNI, and service meshes. Contents The Kubernetes Networking Model Services Ingress & Gateway API Cluster DNS Network Policies CNI Plugins Service Meshes Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet 1. The Kubernetes Networking Model Kubernetes enforces four fundamental networking requirements: Every Pod gets its own IP address and can communicate with every other Pod without NAT. Nodes can communicate with all Pods without NAT. The IP a Pod sees itself as is the same IP others see it as. Services provide stable virtual IPs that load-balance across Pod backends. This flat, routable Pod network is implemented by a CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin on each node. Common choices: Calico, Cilium, Flannel, AWS VPC CNI, Azure CNI. The Pod addresses come from a Pod CIDR range (for example 10.244.0.0/16 ), usually cut into one slice per node. Pick it so it never overlaps your cloud networks, office, or VPN. See planning addresses for Kubernetes for the subnet math. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Node 10.0.1.5 │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ │ Pod 10.244.1.3│ │ Pod 10.244.1.4│ │ Pod 10.244.1.5│ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ └─────────────────┴─────────────────┘ │ │ │ bridge / overlay (CNI) │ │ kubelet + container runtime │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Pod-to-Pod traffic routes across nodes via CNI overlay or cloud VPC routing - no port mapping required. Key distinction: A Service is a stable abstraction (virtual IP + DNS name). Pods are ephemeral - their IPs change on every restart. Always route traffic to Services, not directly to Pod IPs. 2. Services A Service is a stable network endpoint that selects Pods by label and load-balances traffic to them. kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS rules on every node to implement the Service virtual IP (ClusterIP). This is Layer 4 balancing: a pod is chosen once per TCP connection, so long-lived HTTP/2 and gRPC connections can pin all traffic to one pod (see the gRPC one-pod scenario ). Service types Type Reachable from Typical use ClusterIP (default) Inside cluster only Internal microservices, databases NodePort External via NodeIP : port Dev, bare-metal without cloud LB LoadBalancer External via cloud LB Production public APIs on EKS/GKE/AKS ExternalName DNS CNAME to external host Proxy to SaaS or legacy systems Headless ( clusterIP: None ) Direct Pod DNS records StatefulSets, client-side LB ClusterIP Service apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: api namespace: production spec: type: ClusterIP selector: app: api tier: backend ports: - name: http port: 80 # Service port (what clients connect to) targetPort: 8080 # Container port (where app listens) protocol: TCP sessionAffinity: None # or ClientIP for sticky sessions NodePort Service apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: api-nodeport spec: type: NodePort selector: app: api ports: - port: 80 targetPort: 8080 nodePort: 30080 # must be 30000–32767; auto-assigned if omitted LoadBalancer Service apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: api-lb annotations: service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "nlb" service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: "internet-facing" spec: type: LoadBalancer selector: app: api ports: - port: 443 targetPort: 8443 Headless Service (StatefulSet pattern) apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: postgres spec: clusterIP: None # headless - no virtual IP selector: app: postgres ports: - port: 5432 # DNS returns individual Pod A records: # postgres-0.postgres.default.svc.cluster.local # postgres-1.postgres.default.svc.cluster.local Endpoints and EndpointSlices When you create a Service, Kubernetes automatically creates Endpoints (or EndpointSlices in newer clusters) listing the IP:port of every matching Pod. If no Pods match the selector, the Endpo

pages.text: Operators & Custom Resources Kubernetes operators from zero: what a controller is, the reconcile loop, watches, informers and work queues, level vs edge triggering, writing a CustomResourceDefinition with a schema, status and printer columns, a toy... Contents The Idea: a Robot That Keeps Things True Words You Need How Built-In Controllers Work Level-Triggered, Not Edge-Triggered Adding a New Kind: the CRD Lab: A Toy Operator Owner References and Cascading Delete Finalizers, and Objects Stuck in Terminating Status, Conditions and observedGeneration A Real Operator in Python (kopf) Running an Operator Safely Operators You Will Meet When Not to Write One Common Pitfalls Practice Problems Cheat Sheet Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution 1. The Idea: a Robot That Keeps Things True Think of a thermostat. You set the desired temperature: 22 C. The thermostat keeps reading the actual temperature. If it is too cold, it turns on the heater. If it is too warm, it turns it off. It never stops checking. You never tell it "heat for 10 minutes"; you only say what you want. Kubernetes is built from many small thermostats called controllers . You write "I want 3 copies of this pod" in YAML. The ReplicaSet controller keeps counting pods and creating or deleting them until there are 3. An operator is the same idea for something Kubernetes does not know about. You write: apiVersion: db.example.com/v1 kind: Database metadata: name: orders-db spec: replicas: 3 version: "17" backupSchedule: "0 2 * * *" and a program you install in the cluster turns that into pods, services, volumes, a backup CronJob, and a failover plan, and keeps them right forever. It encodes what a human database admin would do, which is where the name comes from: it replaces a human operator . you write: the operator does, again and again: +-----------------+ +-----------------------------------+ | kind: Database | watch | read desired state (spec) | | replicas: 3 | --------- | read actual state (pods, PVCs...) | +-----------------+ | make one step toward desired | ^ | write what it saw into status | | status: ready 3/3 +-----------------------------------+ +-------------------------------------| 2. Words You Need Resource. A kind of object the API server stores, like Pod or Service. Each object has spec (what you want) and usually status (what is true now). Controller. A program that watches some resources and acts to make actual state match desired state. Reconcile. One pass of "compare desired with actual, then fix the difference". The function that does it is the reconciler . CRD (CustomResourceDefinition). An object that tells the API server about a brand new resource kind, like Database . After it is created, you can kubectl get databases . Custom resource (CR). One object of that new kind, like orders-db . Operator. CRDs plus a controller that manages them. Usually it carries expert knowledge about one piece of software. Watch. A long-lived request to the API server that streams every change to a set of objects. Idempotent. Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. A reconciler must be idempotent. Owner reference. A note on an object that says "I belong to that other object". Used for automatic cleanup. Finalizer. A label-like string on an object that blocks its deletion until a controller has done its cleanup and removed the string. 3. How Built-In Controllers Work When you scale a Deployment from 3 to 5, nobody sends "create 2 pods" anywhere. Here is the chain: kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=5 | v API server stores Deployment web: spec.replicas = 5 (in etcd) | watch event v Deployment controller: "web wants 5; its ReplicaSet says 3" - updates ReplicaSet web-7d9f: spec.replicas = 5 | watch event v ReplicaSet controller: "web-7d9f wants 5; I see 3 pods with its labels" - creates 2 Pod objects (no node yet) | watch event v Scheduler: picks a node for each new pod | watch event v kubelet on that node: starts the containers, reports status Every arro

Contents The Big Picture The Words, in Plain English How Much Room Does a Node Have? Allocatable Filter, Then Score: a Worked Example Choosing Nodes: nodeSelector and Node Affinity Keeping Pods Away: Taints and Tolerations Pods Near or Far from Other Pods Topology Spread Constraints and Skew Priority and Preemption When a Node Runs Short: Eviction Order Reading a FailedScheduling Message A Full Example (Validated) Common Pitfalls Practice Problems (with Solutions) Cheat Sheet Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution 1. The Big Picture The scheduler is a program in the control plane. It watches for pods that have no node yet. For each one it does three things: new pod (spec.nodeName is empty) │ ▼ 1. FILTER drop every node that CANNOT run the pod (not enough free CPU/memory, taint not tolerated, affinity rule not met, spread rule broken, ...) │ 0 nodes left? ─► pod stays Pending (+ maybe preemption, section 9) ▼ 2. SCORE give each remaining node 0-100 per scoring rule, add the weighted scores, pick the highest │ ▼ 3. BIND write spec.nodeName = chosen node │ ▼ the kubelet on that node sees the pod and starts its containers The scheduler only chooses . It does not start containers, and it never moves a running pod. If conditions change later (a node fills up, a label changes), running pods stay where they are. Intuition. Think of a hotel front desk. First it removes rooms that cannot work (too small, wrong floor, under repair). Then it ranks the rest (quiet side, near the lift) and gives you the best. Once you are in the room, the desk does not move you, even if a better room frees up. 2. The Words, in Plain English Word Meaning Request How much CPU and memory a container says it needs. The scheduler reserves this much on the node. Capacity The total CPU and memory of the machine. Allocatable The part of capacity that pods may reserve, after the system takes its share. Label A key=value tag on an object, like disktype=ssd or topology.kubernetes.io/zone=zone-a . Taint A "keep out" mark on a node . Pods are repelled unless they tolerate it. Toleration A pass on a pod that lets it ignore a matching taint. Affinity A rule that attracts a pod to certain nodes, or to (or away from) other pods. Topology domain A group of nodes that share a label value: one zone, one rack, or one node (by hostname). Skew How uneven a spread is: pods in the fullest domain minus pods in the emptiest one. Priority A number on a pod. Higher-priority pods are scheduled first and may push out lower ones. Preemption Removing lower-priority pods from a node to make room for a higher-priority pod. Eviction The kubelet (or an API call) stopping a pod and removing it from its node. 3. How Much Room Does a Node Have? Allocatable A node with 4 CPUs and 16 GiB of memory does not offer all of it to pods. The operating system, the kubelet and the container runtime need some, and the kubelet keeps a small safety margin for evictions: allocatable = capacity - system-reserved - kube-reserved - eviction threshold Worked example. Capacity 4 CPU (4000m) and 16 GiB (16384 Mi). Reserved: system 100m CPU and 1 GiB, kube 100m CPU and 1 GiB. Hard eviction threshold: 100 Mi of memory (the default memory.available 100Mi ). CPU: 4000m - 100m - 100m = 3800m . Memory: 16384 - 1024 - 1024 - 100 = 14236 Mi (about 13.9 GiB). See the real values with: kubectl describe node worker-1 # look at "Capacity", "Allocatable", and "Allocated resources" The scheduler checks requests , not real use. A pod fits if: sum of requests of pods already on the node + this pod's request = allocatable So a node can be "full" while its CPUs sit at 10% use, because pods requested far more than they use. And a pod with no requests always "f

pages.description: Kubernetes storage: Volumes, PersistentVolumes, PVCs, StorageClasses, CSI drivers, and StatefulSet storage patterns.
pages.text: Kubernetes Storage Kubernetes storage: Volumes, PersistentVolumes, PVCs, StorageClasses, CSI drivers, and StatefulSet storage patterns. Contents Volume Types Overview PersistentVolumes & PVCs StorageClasses & Dynamic Provisioning CSI Drivers StatefulSet Storage Patterns Backup & Restore Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet 1. Volume Types Overview Volume Lifetime Use case emptyDir Pod lifetime Scratch space, sidecar log sharing configMap / secret Pod lifetime Config files, credentials as files hostPath Node filesystem Node-level daemons (avoid for apps) persistentVolumeClaim Independent of Pod Databases, any persistent data projected Pod lifetime Combine multiple sources into one mount emptyDir volumes: - name: cache emptyDir: medium: Memory # tmpfs - fast, not persisted to disk sizeLimit: 256Mi - name: scratch emptyDir: {} # backed by node disk configMap as volume volumes: - name: nginx-config configMap: name: nginx-config items: - key: nginx.conf path: nginx.conf volumeMounts: - name: nginx-config mountPath: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf subPath: nginx.conf readOnly: true 2. PersistentVolumes and PVCs Storage in Kubernetes follows a two-layer model: PersistentVolume (PV) - cluster-level storage resource (like a disk) PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) - Pod's request for storage (like a claim ticket) ┌─────────────┐ binds to ┌─────────────┐ used by ┌─────────────┐ │ PVC │ ──────────▶ │ PV │ ◀────────── │ Pod │ │ (request) │ │ (resource) │ │ (consumer) │ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ Static PV (admin pre-provisions) apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolume metadata: name: pv-nfs-001 spec: capacity: storage: 100Gi accessModes: - ReadWriteMany persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain storageClassName: nfs nfs: server: nfs.example.com path: /exports/data PVC apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: postgres-data namespace: production spec: accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce storageClassName: gp3 resources: requests: storage: 50Gi Access modes Mode Abbreviation Meaning ReadWriteOnce RWO One node can mount read-write (most block storage) ReadOnlyMany ROX Many nodes read-only ReadWriteMany RWX Many nodes read-write (NFS, EFS, CephFS) ReadWriteOncePod RWOP Single Pod only (K8s 1.22+) Reclaim policies Retain - PV kept after PVC deleted; data preserved, manual cleanup required Delete - PV and underlying storage deleted when PVC is deleted (default for dynamic) Recycle - deprecated; scrubs data and makes PV available again Using PVC in a Pod apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: postgres-0 spec: containers: - name: postgres image: postgres:16 volumeMounts: - name: data mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data volumes: - name: data persistentVolumeClaim: claimName: postgres-data 3. StorageClasses and Dynamic Provisioning Dynamic provisioning automatically creates a PV when a PVC is created - no admin pre-provisioning needed. A StorageClass defines the provisioner and parameters. apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1 kind: StorageClass metadata: name: gp3 annotations: storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com parameters: type: gp3 iops: "3000" throughput: "125" encrypted: "true" volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer # delay binding until Pod scheduled allowVolumeExpansion: true reclaimPolicy: Delete volumeBindingMode Immediate - PV provisioned and bound as soon as PVC is created WaitForFirstConsumer - waits until a Pod using the PVC is scheduled, then provisions in the correct AZ (recommended for cloud block storage) # List storage classes kubectl get storageclass # Check PVC status kubectl get pvc -A kubectl describe pvc postgres-data # Expand PVC (requires allowVolumeExpansion: true) kubectl patch pvc postgres-data -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"100Gi"}}}}' 4. CSI Drivers The Container Storage Interface (CSI) is the standard plugin API for storage vendors. CSI drivers run as Pods in the cluster and handle create/mount/snapshot/resize operations. # Common CSI drivers # AWS: ebs.csi.aws.co

pages.title: Debugging Pods: Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff
pages.description: A beginner's playbook for broken Kubernetes pods: the pod lifecycle and where each failure appears, the five commands that solve most cases, Pending, ContainerCreating, ErrImagePull and ImagePullBackOff...
headings: A Pod's Life, and Where It Can Break
Walkthrough: a Release Stuck in a Crash Loop
pages.text: Debugging Pods: Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff A beginner's playbook for broken Kubernetes pods: the pod lifecycle and where each failure appears, the five commands that solve most cases, Pending, ContainerCreating, ErrImagePull and ImagePullBackOff... Contents A Pod's Life, and Where It Can Break The Words, in Plain English The Five Commands Find Your STATUS Pending Stuck in ContainerCreating ErrImagePull and ImagePullBackOff CreateContainerConfigError CrashLoopBackOff and the Back-off Math Exit Codes, Decoded Running but Not Ready Stuck in Terminating Getting Inside: kubectl debug Walkthrough: a Release Stuck in a Crash Loop Common Pitfalls Practice Problems (with Solutions) Cheat Sheet Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution Solution 1. A Pod's Life, and Where It Can Break A pod goes through the same steps every time. Each failure state belongs to one step: kubectl apply │ 1. SCHEDULE scheduler picks a node ─► fails as: Pending │ 2. PREPARE network + volumes set up ─► fails as: ContainerCreating (stuck) │ 3. PULL image downloaded ─► fails as: ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff │ 4. CONFIGURE env from ConfigMap/Secret ─► fails as: CreateContainerConfigError │ 5. RUN your process runs ─► fails as: Error, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled │ 6. READY readiness probe passes ─► fails as: Running but READY 0/1 │ serving traffic ... later, 7. STOP ─► fails as: Terminating (stuck) Intuition. Debugging a pod is like finding where a parcel got stuck. "Not yet shipped" (Pending), "at the depot" (ContainerCreating), "wrong address" (image not found), "opened and returned" (crash). The status tells you the step, so you only need to look at that step. Steps 1 to 4 fail before your code runs , so your app's logs are empty. The answer is in events . Step 5 onward fails in your code , so the answer is usually in the logs . 2. The Words, in Plain English Word Meaning Phase The pod's overall stage: Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, or Unknown. Container state Each container is Waiting, Running, or Terminated. The reason (like CrashLoopBackOff ) is what kubectl get pods shows in STATUS. Event A short message Kubernetes records about an object ("pulled image", "back-off restarting"). Kept for about one hour by default. Restart count How many times the kubelet restarted a container in this pod. Exit code The number a process returns when it ends. 0 means success; anything else is a failure. Back-off Waiting longer and longer between retries, so a broken thing is not retried thousands of times a minute. Signal A message the operating system sends to a process. SIGTERM means "please stop"; SIGKILL means "stop now" and cannot be ignored. Finalizer A "do not delete yet" note on an object. A controller must remove it before the object really goes away. 3. The Five Commands # 1. What state is it in? (-o wide also shows the node and pod IP) kubectl get pods -o wide # 2. Why? Events at the bottom, container state and last state in the middle kubectl describe pod pod # 3. What did the app print? --previous = the container that just crashed kubectl logs pod --previous kubectl logs pod -c container # pick a container if there are several # 4. What happened around it, in time order? kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp # 5. Let me look inside kubectl debug -it pod --image=busybox:1.36 --target= container The single most useful habit: when a container keeps restarting, kubectl logs shows the new , maybe empty, container. Add --previous to see the one that crashed. 4. Find Your STATUS STATUS you see Step that failed Look at Go to Pending Schedule Events: FailedScheduling Section 5 ContainerCreating for minutes Prepare Events: FailedMount, FailedCreatePodSandBox Section 6 ErrImagePull , ImagePullBackOff Pull Events: Failed to pull image Section 7 CreateContainerConfigError Configure Events / describe: missing Secret or key Section 8 Error , CrashLoopBackOff Run logs --previous , Last State, exit code Section 9 OOMKilled Run (memory limit) Las

pages.text: Kubernetes Workloads Kubernetes workloads: Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs, probes, HPA, and resource limits. Contents Pods ReplicaSets Deployments StatefulSets DaemonSets Jobs & CronJobs Probes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) Resource Requests & Limits Cheat Sheet 1. Pods A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP), IPC, and optionally volumes. Most production apps run inside Deployments, but understanding Pods is essential. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Pod 10.244.1.8 │ │ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ │ │ app │ │ sidecar │ │ │ │ :8080 │ │ (logging) │ │ │ └─────────────┘ └─────────────┘ │ │ shared: localhost, volumes, hostname │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Single-container Pod apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: nginx labels: app: nginx spec: containers: - name: nginx image: nginx:1.25 ports: - containerPort: 80 resources: requests: cpu: 100m memory: 128Mi limits: cpu: 500m memory: 256Mi Multi-container Pod (sidecar pattern) apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: app-with-logger spec: containers: - name: app image: myapp:1.0 volumeMounts: - name: logs mountPath: /var/log/app - name: log-shipper image: fluent/fluent-bit:2.2 volumeMounts: - name: logs mountPath: /var/log/app readOnly: true volumes: - name: logs emptyDir: {} Pod lifecycle phases Phase Meaning Pending Accepted but not yet running (scheduling, image pull) Running At least one container is running Succeeded All containers terminated successfully (Jobs) Failed At least one container failed Unknown Node communication lost Do not manage Pods directly in production. Pods are ephemeral. Use a controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, Job) so Kubernetes recreates them when nodes fail or updates roll out. 2. ReplicaSets A ReplicaSet maintains a stable set of Pod replicas. It creates or deletes Pods to match spec.replicas and uses a label selector to identify managed Pods. apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: ReplicaSet metadata: name: api-rs labels: app: api spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: api tier: backend template: metadata: labels: app: api tier: backend spec: containers: - name: api image: myregistry/api:1.0.0 ports: - containerPort: 8080 You rarely create ReplicaSets directly. Deployments own ReplicaSets and handle rolling updates. ReplicaSets remain the mechanism underneath. kubectl get rs kubectl describe rs api-rs # Pods owned by ReplicaSet show ownerReferences in metadata 3. Deployments A Deployment is the standard way to run stateless applications. It manages ReplicaSets and supports declarative updates, rollbacks, and scaling. Basic Deployment apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: api namespace: production spec: replicas: 3 revisionHistoryLimit: 5 selector: matchLabels: app: api template: metadata: labels: app: api spec: containers: - name: api image: myregistry/api:2.0.0 ports: - containerPort: 8080 Rolling update strategy spec: strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: maxSurge: 1 # extra Pods above desired count during update maxUnavailable: 0 # zero-downtime: always keep full capacity minReadySeconds: 10 # Rollout commands kubectl set image deployment/api api=myregistry/api:2.1.0 kubectl rollout status deployment/api kubectl rollout history deployment/api kubectl rollout undo deployment/api kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=2 Recreate strategy (brief downtime) spec: strategy: type: Recreate # kill all old Pods, then start new ones Deployment revision diagram Deployment "api" (desired: 3 replicas, image v2) │ ├── ReplicaSet api-7d4f8b (rev 2, image v2) ← active, 3 Pods └── ReplicaSet api-9a2c1e (rev 1, image v1) ← scaled to 0, kept for rollback 4. StatefulSets StatefulSets manage stateful applications with stable network identities, ordered deployment, and persistent storage per replica. Use for databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper, Elasticsearch. pages.description: All key equations in one place for quick revision.
pages.text: GNN Formula Sheet All key equations in one place for quick revision. Graph Matrices Message Passing (MPNN) GCN GraphSAGE GAT GIN ChebNet R-GCN Knowledge Graph Embeddings Homophily Link Prediction Loss Graph Matrices $$\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$$ $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{sym}} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$$ $$\mathbf{f}^T \mathbf{L} \mathbf{f} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{(i,j) \in E} (f_i - f_j)^2$$ $$\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{D}^{-1/2}(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{I})\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}$$ Message Passing (MPNN) $$\mathbf{m}_{ij}^{(l+1)} = \phi^{(l)}\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)}, \mathbf{h}_j^{(l)}, \mathbf{e}_{ij}\right)$$ $$\bar{\mathbf{m}}_i^{(l+1)} = \bigoplus_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \mathbf{m}_{ij}^{(l+1)}$$ $$\mathbf{h}_i^{(l+1)} = \gamma^{(l)}\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)}, \bar{\mathbf{m}}_i^{(l+1)}\right)$$ $$\mathbf{h}_G = \text{READOUT}\left(\{\mathbf{h}_i^{(L)}\}\right)$$ GCN $$\mathbf{H}^{(l+1)} = \sigma\left(\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \mathbf{H}^{(l)} \mathbf{W}^{(l)}\right)$$ GraphSAGE $$\mathbf{h}_i^{(l+1)} = \sigma\left(\mathbf{W}^{(l)} \cdot \text{CONCAT}\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)}, \text{AGG}(\{\mathbf{h}_j^{(l)}\}_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)})\right)\right)$$ GAT $$e_{ij} = \text{LeakyReLU}\left(\vec{a}^T [\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_i \| \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_j]\right)$$ $$\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \exp(e_{ik})}$$ $$\mathbf{h}_i^{(l+1)} = \sigma\left(\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \alpha_{ij} \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_j^{(l)}\right)$$ GIN $$\mathbf{h}_i^{(l+1)} = \text{MLP}^{(l)}\left((1 + \epsilon^{(l)}) \mathbf{h}_i^{(l)} + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \mathbf{h}_j^{(l)}\right)$$ ChebNet $$\mathbf{g} * \mathbf{f} \approx \sum_{k=0}^{K} \theta_k T_k(\tilde{\mathbf{L}})\mathbf{f}$$ R-GCN $$\mathbf{h}_i^{(l+1)} = \sigma\left(\sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_r(i)} \frac{1}{c_{i,r}} \mathbf{W}_r^{(l)} \mathbf{h}_j^{(l)} + \mathbf{W}_0^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)}\right)$$ Knowledge Graph Embeddings TransE: $\|\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{t}\|$ DistMult: $\langle \mathbf{h}, \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t} \rangle$ Homophily $$h = \frac{|\{(u,v) : (u,v) \in E \land y_u = y_v\}|}{|E|}$$ Link Prediction Loss $$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{(i,j) \in E^+} \log \sigma(\mathbf{h}_i^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{h}_j) - \sum_{(i,j) \in E^-} \log(1 - \sigma(\mathbf{h}_i^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{h}_j))$$
